IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

Transfer Petition (Civil) No. 3489/2025
VAISHNAVI RAGESH                             Petitioner(s)
                           VERSUS
GAUTAM KUMAR ANIL KUMAR                      Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. The petitioner has filed the petition under Section
25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 before this Court
seeking transfer of the case, details of which are as
under:
“OP (Others) 1144/2025 titled as “Gautam Kumar
Anil Kumar vs. Vaishnavi Ragesh” from the Family
Court, Attingal, Kerala to the court of competent
jurisdiction at Bardoli, Surat, Gujarat.”  
2. During the pendency of aforesaid transfer petition,
the parties were referred to the Supreme Court Mediation
Centre  vide  order dated 26.02.2026. By virtue of the
mediation, the parties have arrived at a settlement and
they have decided to part ways on certain terms and
conditions which are delineated in the settlement agreement
dated 16.07.2026 which has been signed by both the parties,
copy of which has been filed by the Supreme Court Mediation
Centre.
3. Learned counsel for the parties have filed a joint
application  bearing  IA  No.  315537  of  2026  with  the
1

--- Page 36 ---
following prayer:
“a)  Quash/Set Aside all the cases and proceedings
pending between the parties;
b) Dissolve the marriage of the parties by a decree
of  divorce  by  mutual  consent  under  the  Hindu
Marriage  Act  in  exercise  of  the  extra-ordinary
powers under Article 142 of the Constitution of
India;”
4. Further, the terms and conditions and the relevant
paragraphs  as  set  out  in  Settlement  Agreement  dated
16.07.2026 are as under: 
“SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT
This settlement agreement is executed on this the 16 th
day of July 2026 at Kerala between
Vaishnavi Ragesh aged 30 yrs D/o Ragesh Raghuvaran,

And Gautam Kumar Anil Kumar S/o Anilkumar K.P. R/o

Represented  by  his  Power  of  Attorney  Holder  and

Sherly  Bhavanam,  Mylamkulam,  Puthoor  P.O  Puthoor

the SECOND PARTY
WHEREAS:
1. The marriage between the First Party and the
Second  Party  was  solemnised  on  17.04.2022  in

--- Page 37 ---

(i) Maintenance Petition bearing No. CRMAJ No.

(iii) Transfer Petition (C) No. 3489 of 2025,

4. The Second Party has filed a Original Petition
bearing OP No. 1144/2025, pending before the Family
Court, Attingal. (CNR No. KLTV410014932025 Filing No.
1490/2025)
5. The First Party instituted Transfer Petition (C)
No. 3489 of 2025 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of
India seeking transfer of Original Petition OP No.
1144/2025, pending before the Family Court, Attingal
to family court in Surat.
6. At  the  time  of  hearing  of  the  said  Transfer

referred the matter to mediation before the Supreme

on  13.03.2026,  30/03/2026,  03.04.2026,  16.04.2026,

15.07.2026  through  virtual  mode,  in  languages

in this mediation through online mode along with his
father Mr. Anilkumar K.P. The Second Party has issued

TERMS OF SETTLEMENT
1. The  parties  agree  that  their  marriage  has
irretrievably  broken  down  due  to  irreconcilable
differences and that it is not possible for them to
live  together  as  husband  and  wife.  The  parties
mutually  agree  to  part  ways  amicably  by  seeking
dissolution of marriage.

agrees to pay a lump sum amount of Rs.50,00,000/-

towards full and final settlement of all her claims,

The parties agree that the terms, conditions, and

5. We have taken the Joint Application and Settlement

exercising power under Article 142 of the Constitution of
India  to  dissolve  the  marriage  between  the  parties.
Consequently, the marriage between the parties which was
solemnized on 17.04.2022 stands dissolved by a decree of
divorce by mutual consent.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.           /2026
[@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO.5531/2026]
NEELAM YADAV                                   APPELLANT(S)
                           VERSUS
STATE OF U.P. & ANR.                          RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties. 
3. This appeal impugns the judgment and order of the High
Court1 dated 16.02.2026 in Criminal Revision No.957 of
2026 whereby appellant’s revision against the order of
Trial Court2 dated 03.01.2026 summoning the appellant
under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure,
19733 for being tried along with other accused in
S.T.4 No.463 of 2022, has been dismissed.
4. On 25.07.2022 at about 11.25 hrs. a First Information
1 1 High Court of Judicature at Allahabad 
2 2 Additional Sessions Judge (First), Lalitpur 3 3 CrPC
4 4 Sessions Trial
1

--- Page 56 ---
Report (for short, FIR) was registered at Police
Station Jakhaura, District Lalitpur under Section 302
of the Indian Penal Code, 18605 arraigning Raman Singh
and Neelam Yadav (i.e. the appellant) as accused.  In
the FIR it was alleged that on 23.07.2022, at about
21.30 hrs., Raman Singh i.e. brother of the informant
along with the appellant came to informant’s house and
demanded his share from the deceased i.e. Bhagwan
Singh, the father of the informant and Raman Singh.
When the deceased refused to execute the transfer
instrument, the appellant held hand of the deceased
and Raman Singh stabbed the deceased with a knife and
thereafter  both  fled.  It  was  alleged  that  the
informant was involved in his father’s cremation,
therefore, could not report earlier. 
5. After investigation, chargesheet was laid only against
Raman Singh.  During trial, after recording statements
of PW1, PW2 and PW3, an application was submitted
under Section 319 CrPC to arraign the appellant as an
accused. The Trial Court vide order dated 25.06.2025
summoned the appellant for being tried along with
other  accused.  Aggrieved  therewith,  the  appellant
filed a criminal revision before the High Court which
5 5 IPC
2

--- Page 57 ---
stood dismissed by the impugned order.
6. The submission on behalf of the appellant is that the
Trial Court has mechanically exercised its power under
Section 319 CrPC without even applying its mind to the
entire deposition of the witnesses. It is submitted
that had the Trial Court considered the testimony of
the witnesses in its entirety including what they
stated during cross-examination, it may not have found
it appropriate to summon the appellant at all. It is
submitted  that  during  cross-examination,  PW1  had
stated that he had not personally witnessed anyone
attacking his father and that he did not lodge First
Information Report on the day of the incident rather
it was lodged upon insistence of the villagers.  It
was stated by him that he mentioned the name of Raman
Singh and Neelam on being prompted by the villagers
and that he did not see Raman Singh with Neelam. It is
submitted that the other witness PW2 was declared
hostile. Likewise, the third witness (PW3) was also
declared  hostile  by  the  prosecution.  In  such
circumstances, the submission is that the Trial Court
has mechanically exercised its power without applying
its mind to the evidence collected thus far. It is
urged that the power under Section 319 CrPC is to be
3

--- Page 58 ---
sparingly exercised when a case more than a  prima
facie case is made out. Therefore, when PW1 in  his
deposition during cross-examination had stated that
the incident did not occur in his presence and that he
had lodged the FIR at the insistence of the villagers,
there was no justification for the Trial Court to have
overlooked that part of the statement before taking a
decision whether to arraign additional accused in the
exercise of power conferred upon it by Section 319 of
CrPC.  Accordingly, it was prayed that the impugned
order as well as the summoning order be set aside. 
7. Per  contra,  on  behalf  of  the  respondents  it  is
submitted that at the stage of exercise of power under
Section 319 CrPC the Court is not required to hold a
mini trial so as to conclude whether the evidence
would ultimately result in conviction. The Court is
merely to be satisfied whether, based on the evidence
available on the record, the additional accused (i.e.,
the one sought to be arraigned as an additional
accused) must be tried along with the one already
facing trial. It is submitted that the statement in
chief of PW-1 indicted both the undertrial accused as
well as the appellant, therefore the exercise of power
under Section 319 CrPC cannot be faulted.   
4

--- Page 59 ---
8. We  have  accorded  due  consideration  to  the  rival
submissions and have perused the record. 
9. One of the objects of vesting power in the Trial Court
to arraign an additional accused under Section 319 of
CrPC is to ensure that a person involved in the crime
does not escape the clutches of law on account of
lapses on the part of investigating agency. However,
this power is to be exercised sparingly based on the
evidence led during trial. We are conscious of the law
that the expression evidence as used in Section 319
CrPC is not confined to the statement of a witness
tested by cross-examination. The power under Section
319 CrPC can very well be exercised based on a
statement-in-chief of a witness, without awaiting his
cross-examination. However, where the witness has been
cross-examined, the trial court cannot shut its eye to
the  entire  statement.  Because  evidence  would  not
merely be the statement in chief of a witness but
would include his statement recorded during cross-
examination. No doubt, the trial court is not supposed
to weigh the statement of a witness on the anvil of
probabilities,  or  against  the  weight  of  other
evidences, to consider whether it would be appropriate
to try the additional accused along with one already
5

--- Page 60 ---
facing trial. However, if the statement of a witness
during cross-examination demolishes the edifice of his
statement in chief, the trial court cannot overlook
the statement in its entirety, when the decision to
arraign  additional  accused  rests  entirely  on  his
statement; though, after considering the statement in
its entirety, it would be within the domain of the
Trial Court whether to arraign the additional accused
to face trial along with the one already facing trial.
10. As we find that neither the High Court nor the Trial
Court has considered the deposition of the witnesses,
particularly  of  PW1,  in  its  entirety,  and  have
overlooked the statement of PW-1 made during cross-
examination, we are of the view that the order of the
Trial Court as well as the High Court is liable to be
set aside. However, there shall be liberty to the
Trial Court to consider the request for arraigning
additional accused afresh, and in accordance with law.
11. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed.  The impugned
order(s) of the High Court as well as the Trial Court
are hereby set aside.
12. The Trial Court would, however, be at liberty to
reconsider  the  prayer  for  arraigning  additional
accused in accordance with law.
6

--- Page 61 ---
13. We make it clear that we have not expressed our
opinion  on  the  merits  of  the  prosecution  case/
evidence. 
14. All  pending  applications  including  the  one
seeking impleadment are disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.        /2026
  [@ SLP [CRL.] NO.16408/2024]
GURMEJ SINGH                         Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ORS.                Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. In 2012, the appellant herein was convicted for
murder in the United Kingdom and was sentenced to
undergo life imprisonment by the Crown Court at
Birmingham, with minimum tariff of 35 years. In
other words, the appellant stood convicted, and
accordingly, was sentenced for a minimum period of
35 years under the United Kingdom laws. Thereafter,
he applied for transfer to India under the Indo-UK
Agreement on Transfer of Sentenced Persons (for
short  ‘the  Indo-UK  Agreement').   On  a  doubt
expressed by the UK authorities, the Government of
India sent a communication dated 20.06.2018, which
states as under:
“Insofar as the specific issue raised by you
in the letter under reference is concerned,
it is informed that the UK Government vide
their  letter  dated  6th October,  2008  had
asked  MHA  seeking  confirmation  about
“continued  enforcement”  of  the  sentence

--- Page 73 ---
2
awarded to Mr. Rai.  In response to UK Govt’s
letter, Govt. of India has informed that in
the  event  of  his  transfer,  there  is  a
possibility of invoking provision of Article
8(2) of the Indo-UK TSP agreement and thereby
adapting Mr. Rai’s sentence to make the same
compatible with the Indian law.  It was also
informed that as per Indian law, Mr. Rai
would  be  considered  for  release  by  the
Sentence  Review  Board  after  14  years  of
imprisonment. To this, UK authorities had
responded  that  since  this  will  provide
benefit to Mr. Rai for a possible 21 years
reduction in his tariff, they wold refuse
transfer  of  Mr.  Rai  on  these  terms.
Subsequently, the Govt. of India had replied
to the UK Govt.(copy attached) the Hon’ble
Supreme Court of India had clarified that a
convict  undergoing  life  imprisonment  is
expected to remain in custody till the end of
his natural life subject to remission granted
by the appropriate Government under the law.
Thereafter, the transfer was agreed by the UK
side and Mr. Gurmej Singh was transferred to
India  on  15.05.2015.  Relevant  papers/UK
Court’s Judgment related to the case of Mr.
Gurmej Singh are attached.”
3. Accordingly, the appellant was transferred and
made to undergo his sentence in the State of Punjab.
The appellant made an application for premature
release upon completion of 14 years, which was
rejected by the Government of India.
4. Aggrieved,  he  filed  a  writ  petition,  being

--- Page 74 ---
3
CR.W.P. No.218 of 2023, before the High Court. The
High Court, vide order dated 31.10.2023, upheld the
decision taken by the respondent No.2, inter alia,
holding  that  the  appellant  had  to  undergo  the
remaining period of sentence, as awarded by the UK
Court.  Aggrieved by the same, the appellant is
before us.
5. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  appellant
submitted that on a combined reading of Sections
13(6), 11 and 12 of the Repatriation of Prisoners
Act, 2003, on one hand and Articles 8 and 10 of the
Indo-UK Agreement on the other, the impugned order
of  the  High  Court  and  the  one  passed  by  the
respondent No.2 cannot be sustained in the eyes of
law.
6. In  support  of  his  submission,  the  learned
counsel for the appellant placed reliance on a
decision of this Court in Criminal Appeal No.2084 of
2023 dated 24.07.2023, wherein the following views
were expressed:
“We  have  perused  the  provisions  of  the
Repatriation of the Prisoners Act, 2003 and a
copy of the Transfer of Sentenced Persons
Agreement between the Government of India and
the Government of United Kingdom.  After
having perused the Clause (2) of Article 10
thereof,  we  find  that  there  is  a  power
vesting in Union of India even to grant
pardon, amnesty or commutation of sentence in

--- Page 75 ---
4
accordance with the laws prevailing in India.
We do not see any prohibition on grant of
parole to the appellant on valid and lawful
grounds.”
7. Learned ASG appearing for the Union of India and
the learned counsel appearing for the State would
submit that Article 8 of the Indo-UK Agreement does
not facilitate modification of the sentence imposed,
to the benefit of the appellant.
8. In support of his submission, the learned ASG
placed reliance on a decision of this Court in Union
of India v. Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed & Ors.  - (2022) 13
SCC 380.
9. Having heard the parties, we shall first record
Article 8 and Article 10 of the Indo-UK Agreement
for a better understanding:
“Article 8
Continued enforcement of sentence
1. The receiving State shall be bound by the
legal nature and duration of the sentence as
determined by the transferring State.
2. If, however, the sentence is by its nature
or duration or both incompatible with the law
of  the  receiving  State,  or  its  law  so
requires,  that  State  may,  by  Court  or
administrative order, adapt the sentence to a
punishment or measure prescribed by its own

--- Page 76 ---
5
law.  As to its nature and duration the
punishment  or  measure  shall,  as  far  as
possible, correspond with that imposed by the
judgment of the transferring State.  It shall
however  not  aggravate,  by  its  nature  or
duration,  the  sentence  imposed  in  the
transferring State.
Article 10
Pardon, amnesty or commutation, and review of
judgment
1. The transferring State alone shall decide
on any application for the review of the
judgment.
2. Either  of  the  Contracting  States  may
grant pardon, amnesty or commutation of the
sentence in accordance with its Constitution
or other laws.”
10. We are not concerned with the case of the
appellant coming under Article 8 per se.  Rather,
the present case involves the application of the
relevant remission policy to the appellant. It is
not in dispute that if the same offence had been
committed in India, the appellant would have been
entitled for the said relief.
11. Hence,  the  question  that  arises  for
consideration is as to whether Article 10 of the
Indo-UK Agreement can be pressed into service or
not.
12. A  reading  of  Article  10(2)  of  the  Indo-UK

--- Page 77 ---
6
Agreement would clearly indicate that either of the
contracting States may grant pardon, amnesty and
commutation, in accordance with the Constitution or
other laws. The words “ other laws” would certainly
include the laws governing remission of sentence.
13. It is not as if the conviction  per se  is
modified, but it is only the sentence that stands
reduced, by way of a policy decision in the form of
remission. So long as the said power exists with the
State, it assumes the trapping of "other laws", as
mentioned in Article 10 of the Indo-UK Agreement.
14. The decision relied upon by the learned ASG in
Union  of  India  v.  Shaikh  Istiyaq  Ahmed  &  Ors
(supra), does not apply to the facts of the case.
In  the  said  case,  Article  10  of  the  Indo-UK
Agreement was not involved, since it was a question
of reducing the sentence, as per the sentencing
policy,  corresponding  to  the  offence  committed,
pursuant to the conviction rendered.
15. We also find it apposite to mention that the
communication of the Government of India, Ministry
of Home Affairs dated 20.06.2018, clearly states
that the deportation of the appellant would be
subject to the remission policy of the appropriate
State/Government. 
16. Thus, we have no hesitation in setting aside the
impugned order of the High Court dated 31.10.2023.

--- Page 78 ---
7
17. Accordingly, the order passed by the respondent
No.2 also stands set aside. Respondent No.2 is
directed to consider the case of the appellant
afresh, in accordance with the policy governing,
within a period of eight weeks from the date of
receipt of a copy of this order.
18. The appeal stands disposed of, accordingly.
19. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

1. Leave granted.
2. This appeal is directed against an interim order passed by the Delhi High
Court in W.P.(C) No. 4582/2003, whereby the Appellant’s prayer for extension of time
was rejected.
3. The High Court has, inter alia, declined to interfere with the timeline due to the
successive directions passed by this Court in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 4677/1985 and
connected cases.
4. At this stage, we are faced with two key developments:
4.1 Firstly, the limited prayer of the Appellant before the High Court was to
extend the time granted for completion of the regularisation process. W.P.(C)
No. 4582/2003 has also since been disposed of by the Delhi High Court vide
order dated 26.09.2011. It, thus, seems to us that the Appellant’s prayer made
in 2007 may have become infructuous due to efflux of time.
4.2 Secondly, through a reportable judgement dated 11.03.2026, the issues

--- Page 83 ---
4
forming the subject matter of this appeal now stand transferred to the High
Court. Now, the foundation of the High Court’s observations, namely, that the
clarification must be sought from this Court, no longer exists.
5. Keeping in mind both of the above factors, we deem it appropriate to dispose
of this Appeal as infructuous. The questions of law, if any, raised in this case shall
remain open.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 10378 OF 2017
MUNICIPAL CORPORATION OF DELHI (NORTH)         Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
M/S HARCHARAN DASS GUPTA                       Respondent(s)
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 10380 OF 2017
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 10379 OF 2017
O R D E R 
1. This order shall dispose of the three Civil
Appeals filed by the Municipal Corporation of Delhi
[in short, “the Corporation”]  
C.A.No. 10378 OF 2017 and C. A. No. 10380 OF 2017
2. These two appeals by the Corporation are against
the Judgment and Order dated 08.11.2012 passed by the
High Court of Delhi in FAO (OS) No. 535 of 2012 and
FAO (OS) No. 534 of 2012.
3. The  Municipal  Corporation  and  the  respondent
contractor entered into an Agreement dated 20.04.1992
pursuant to a work order, that was issued in 1991. It

--- Page 89 ---
2
is the case of the respondent that work commenced in
1991 and was completed on 18.09.1992 in FAO (OS) No.
534 of 2012 and on 17.08.1992 in FAO (OS) No. 535 of
2012. Thereafter, the respondent contractor kept on
asking the Municipal Corporation to make the necessary
payment, but as the Corporation was not making the
necessary payments, disputes arose between the parties
and they were referred to the Sole Arbitrator for
adjudication and determination. 
4. Before the Arbitral Tribunal, the Corporation did
not take the plea of limitation at the very outset. It
is also on record that even at the time of arguments
the plea of limitation was not pressed. However, it is
an admitted fact that in the written submissions filed
after the Arbitral Tribunal reserved the case for
Award, the plea of limitation was specifically taken.
Eventually, the Arbitral Tribunal passed its Award
inter alia, rejecting the plea of limitation. 
5. The Corporation filed objections under Section 34
of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act [in short,
“the Act”], and the plea of limitation was raised and
also contested. The learned Single Judge of the High
Court by its judgment dated 09.05.2006, accepted the
said objections and allowed the Section 34 petition
holding that the invocation as well as claims are
barred by limitation.

--- Page 90 ---
3
6. In the Section 37 appeal filed by the respondent,
the Division Bench of the High Court, by the order
impugned before us, set aside the judgment of the
learned Single Judge and remanded the matter back to
the  Arbitral  Tribunal  for  deciding  the  issue  of
limitation afresh after taking necessary evidence on
record. The relevant portion of the order is as
follows:-
“9. We  are  of  the  view  that  the
manner in which the respondents sought
to  slip-in  this  plea  of  bar  of
limitation cannot be appreciated. We are
conscious  that  a  plea  of  bar  of
limitation can be raised at any stage
but given the situation, it was a mixed
question of law and fact. It should have
been  specifically  pleaded  giving  an
opportunity to the appellant to respond
to that plea and the parties ought to
have been given opportunity to produce
the material in support of this plea. We
are not inclined to disturb the findings
of the Arbitrator qua the other aspects,
especially when they have not been dealt
with by the learned Single Judge. We
are,  thus,  of  the  view  that  the
appellant must get full opportunity to
meet this plea and, thus, the impugned
order dated 21.08.2012 is set aside.
10.  The  specific  plea  of  limitation
setting out the relevant facts will be
filed  by  the  respondent  before  the
learned  Arbitrator  within  four  weeks
from today with supporting documents and
the appellant will respond to the same
with  relevant  documents  within  four
weeks thereafter. The matter is remanded
to the Arbitrator for decision on this
limited issue and, in case, the finding
is adverse to the respondent, it will
naturally be open to the respondent to
challenge the said finding as also the
finding on merits, as the learned Single

--- Page 91 ---
4
Judge has not dealt with the objections
on merits filed by the respondent.
11. The record of the Arbitrator, which
is lying in the court, be remitted back
to the Arbitrator. It is agreed that the
record will be collected by the learned
counsel for the respondent in a sealed
cover  to  be  handed  over  to  the
Arbitrator.”
7. Heard Mr. Yatinder Singh, learned senior counsel
assisted  by  Mr.  Praveen  Swarup,  learned  counsel
appearing for the appellant Corporation and Mr. Harish
Malhotra, learned senior counsel assisted by Mr. Dhruv
Kapur, learned counsel appearing for the respondent.
8. Having considered the matter in detail, we are of
the opinion that there was sufficient material on
record for the Division Bench of the High Court,
exercising appellate jurisdiction under Section 37 of
the Act to take a decision on the issue of limitation.
9. We  see  no  justification  whatsoever  for  the
Division Bench to remand the matter back to the
Arbitral Tribunal, particularly when the said Tribunal
considered the issue of limitation in detail and gave
its award. Further, the learned Single Judge of the
High Court also considered the objection under Section
34 of the Act and in fact accepted the plea of
limitation and held that the claims are barred in this
background. The Division Bench of the High Court was
only  exercising  the  appellate  jurisdiction  under

--- Page 92 ---
5
Section 37 of the Act and the material on record,
coupled with the reasoning and conclusion of the
Arbitral Tribunal as well as the High Court under
Section 34 was available to it to arrive at an
appropriate  conclusion  as  regards  the  issue  of
limitation.  We  have  no  doubt  in  our  minds  that
remanding the matter back to the Arbitral Tribunal
after  a  period  of  six  years  is  unnecessary  and
unjustified in the facts and circumstances of the
case. 
10. In view of the above, the C.A. Nos. 10378 of 2017
and 10380 of 2017 are allowed, and the judgment and
order passed by the Division Bench of the High Court
in FAO (OS) No. 535 of 2012 and FAO (OS) No. 534 of
2012 dated 8.11.2012 are set aside and Section 37
appeal(s) before the High Court are restored to their
original number. The High Court will now consider
Section  37  appeal(s)  on  merits,  as  well  as  on
limitation, and decide the appeal(s) in accordance
with law. 
11. In view of the fact that the original reference
to arbitration is of the year 2003, we request the
High Court to take up and dispose of the Section 37
appeal(s) as expeditiously as possible, preferably
within a period of four months from today.
12. Learned counsel for the appellant(s) and the
respondent(s) have agreed to move a joint application

--- Page 93 ---
6
before the High Court for early listing of Section 37
appeal(s). 
13. Pending  interlocutory  application(s),  if  any,
is/are disposed of.
C.A. No. 10379 OF 2017
1. In this appeal by the Municipal Corporation, it
is an admitted fact that the plea of limitation was
not raised at any point of time.
2. Though  Mr.  Yatinder  Singh,  learned  senior
counsel, seeks to submit that such a plea can be
raised for the first time before the Court, we are not
inclined to entertain such a plea in the facts and
circumstances of the case. The question of law raised
by  Mr.  Yatinder  Singh  is  kept  open  for  being
considered in an appropriate case. 
3. The civil appeal is, accordingly, dismissed and
the accompanying interlocutory application(s), if any,
stands disposed of.

                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. We heard Mr. Kapil Sibal and Ms. Meenakshi Arora, the
learned senior counsel appearing for the applicant, Mr. J.
Rajesh, the learned counsel appearing for the respondent
1

--- Page 97 ---
no.1 and Mr. Rajesh Kumar Gautam, the learned counsel
appearing for the respondent no.4 Bank.
3. Our order dated 15.07.2026 reads thus:-
“1. We heard Ms. Meenakshi Arora, the learned senior
counsel appearing for the appellant, Mr. Navin Pahwa, the
learned senior counsel appearing for the respondent no.1
(shareholder), Mr. Rajesh Kumar Gautam, the learned senior
counsel appearing for the Indian Bank. We also heard Mr.
Krishnan Venugopal, the learned senior counsel appearing
for the respondent no.2 and in the last, we also heard Mr.
C.A. Sundaram, the learned senior counsel appearing for a
party, namely, Brightlane Infraspace Pvt. Ltd., who has
some interest in this litigation.
2. In the appeals before us, the following reliefs have
been prayed for:-
“A. Admit and the Allow the instant Civil Appeal
against the impugned judgment and interim orders
dated 17.06.2026 & 29.06.2026 in I.A. No.4230 of
2026 in Company Appeal (AT) No.210 of 2026 passed
by the Hon'ble National Company Law Appellate
Tribunal  Principal  Bench,  New  Delhi  in  the
interest of justice; and 
B. Permit Respondent No. 2 Company to raise
capital by way of a Rights Issue at par offered to
all its existing shareholders in proportion to
their shareholding, in terms of the proposal made
before the Appellate Tribunal, the Appellant and
Respondent  No.  5  being  ready  and  willing  to
contribute the entire amount including to the
extent of any shares remaining unsubscribed;
C. Pass any other order and/or directions, as
this Hon'ble Court may be fit and proper under the
facts and circumstances of the present case”
3. Having regard to the nature of the submissions
canvassed before us, it is difficult for us to adjudicate
the disputed question of fact.
4. The matter is coming up before the NCLAT Principal
Bench, New Delhi on 23.07.2026. It shall be open for all
the concerned to raise all legal contentions available to
them before the NCLAT on 23.07.2026.
5. It shall also be open for the client of Mr. Sundaram
to make his submissions before the NCLAT, if at all, he is
a party before the NCLAT. If the client of Mr. Sundaram is
not a party, he may apply and it is for the NCLAT to
decide whether the client of Mr. Sundaram is a proper or a
necessary party in the proceedings.
2

--- Page 98 ---
6. We make an earnest request to the NCLAT to see that
on 23.07.2026 the matter is heard for sure. We make this
request to the NCLAT because we are informed that NCLT has
reserved the order insofar Section 7 IBC application is
concerned.
7. With the aforesaid, these appeals stand disposed of.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.”
4. By our order referred to above, we had made an earnest
request to the NCLAT to ensure that the main matter is heard
on 23.07.2026. We made this request to the NCLAT considering
that the NCLT had reserved its order insofar as Section 7
IBC application is concerned.
5. Today, the learned senior counsel appearing for the
applicant brought to our notice that the NCLAT has not heard
the matter till this date. They also brought to our notice
that in the meantime, the order that was reserved by the
NCLT has been pronounced and Section 7 IBC application has
been admitted.
6. We are quite disturbed with the manner in which the
NCLAT has conducted itself in the present litigation. The
request made is out of deference to their position and to
ensure that the judicial office they hold is not belittled
in any manner.
7. When the Supreme Court makes a request to any Court or
Tribunal, it has to be construed as a direction and not just
a request. It is one thing that the Supreme Court earnestly
requests in the hope that the Court or the Tribunal would
abide by the request and do the needful. However, today, we
3

--- Page 99 ---
make it very clear that if there is any request made by the
Supreme Court to any Court or Tribunal, the same shall be
treated as a direction and non-compliance of such direction
shall be looked into very seriously.
8. A similar situation arose where the High Court despite
this Court directing the parties to approach that court for
expeditious consideration and expressing that the High Court
would give due attention to the prayer, the Division Bench
of the High Court recorded an order that having considered
the matter, they find no reason to grant precedence. This
Court in  Spencer and Co., Ltd. and Anr v. Vishwadarshan
Distributors Pvt. Ltd. and ors.  reported in 1995 SCC (1)
259, restrained itself, exercising judicial statesmanship
and held so: 
“6. Ex facie courtesy is the blend of our order of 14-1-
1994. Outwardly it is neither commanding in nature nor
explicitly in terms of a direction. Such is not the sheen
and tone of our order, meant as it was, for a high
constitutional  institution,  being  the  High  Court.  It
comes from another high constitutional institution (this
Court) hierarchically superior in the corrective ladder.
When one superior speaks to another it is always in
language sweet, soft and melodious; more suggestive than
directive. Judicial language is always chaste.
7. Traditions and norms in this regard, well-established
and followed in this country since time immemorial, are
best reflected in the “Song Celestial”, the Bhagavad
Gita. It would for the purpose be apposite to turn to the
18th  Chapter  of  the  Bhagavad  Gita,  containing  the
concluding portion of the dialogue between Lord Krishna,
the Best of Beings, (Purushotamma) and Arjuna, the Best
of Humans, (Narotamma), both superiors in themselves.
Verse 63 in the words of Lord Krishna is:
guhyad guhyataram maya
vimrishayaitad eshneshena
yathecchasi tatha kuru
4

--- Page 100 ---
Translation
Thus I have explained to you the most confidential
of all knowledge. Deliberate on this fully, and
then do what you wish to do.
(emphasis ours)
8. Verse 73 containing the answering words of Arjuna
is:
nashto mohah smritir labdha
tvat prasaddan mayachyuta
sthito'smi gata-sandehah
karishye vachanam tava
 Translation
O infallible one, my illusion is now gone. I have
regained my memory by Your mercy, and I am now firm and
free from doubt and am prepared to act according to
Your instructions. 
(emphasis ours)
For Arjuna, the freedom given to act as he wished to,
was  an  illusion;  acting  in  conformity  with  the
instructions of Krishna a bounden duty. This message
has  perceptibly  percolated  down  as  part  of  Indian
culture, philosophy and behavioural setting the tenor
in the Constitution for interaction between the high
constitutional authorities and institutions. One needs
only  to be  aware of  this thought  with which  the
Constitution is soaked.
9. Recently, on a lesser aberration, this Court in
Bayer India Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra [(1993) 3 SCC
29] had occasion to strike a sad note in the following
words: (SCC pp. 31-32, paras 5-6)
“5. We are saddened to notice that in spite of the
Court's request contained in this order dated 6-2-
1991, the High Court has not disposed of the review
petition till now. The High Court was requested to
dispose of the said writ petition within four months
from the date of the said order and, at any rate, by
30-9-1991. It is more than two years since the order
was made. While we certainly respect the independence
of the High Court and recognise that it is a co-equal
institution, we cannot but say, at the same time,
that  the  constitutional  scheme  and  judicial
discipline requires that the High Court should give
due regard to the orders of this Court which are
binding on all courts within the territory of India.
The request made in this case was contained in a
judicial  order.  It  does  no  credit  to  either
institution that it has not been heeded to. We hope
and trust that the delay in the disposal of the
review is either accidental or on account of some or
5

--- Page 101 ---
other procedural problem. Be that as it may, the
present situation would not have arisen if only the
review petition had been disposed of within the time
contemplated in the order dated 6-2-1990.
6. In this view of the matter, the IA is disposed of
with the following directions:
(1) We reiterate our request to the High Court to
dispose of the review petition expeditiously, at any
rate within two months of this order.
(2) (3) ***”
The case which we are dealing with is far more angular
because  there  is  a  deliberate  and  conscious
obstruction, put and recorded by the Hon'ble Judges of
the High Court, even when the judicial order of this
Court dated 14-1-1994 was before them, in support of
the prayer for an early durated hearing of the appeal.
The case in hand is of a negative or reverse action,
whereas Bayer India case [(1993) 3 SCC 29] was barely
of inaction, far less in gravity.
10. The afore-narrated words, we think, presently, are
enough to assert the singular constitutional role of
this Court, and correspondingly of the assisting role
of all authorities, civil or judicial, in the territory
of  India,  towards  it,  who  are  mandated  by  the
Constitution to act in aid of this Court. That the High
Court is one such judicial authority covered under
Article 144 of the Constitution is beyond question. The
order  dated 14-1-1994  of this  Court was  indeed a
judicial order and otherwise enforceable throughout the
territory  of  India  under  Article  142  of  the
Constitution. The High Court was bound to come in aid
of this Court when it required the High Court to have
its order worked out. The language of request oftenly
employed by this Court in such situations is to be read
by the High Court as an obligation, in carrying out the
constitutional mandate, maintaining the writ of this
Court running large throughout the country.”
9. Polite expression does not diminish authority, rather
it enhances, which should never be understood as weakness.
10. We are informed that the next date fixed by the NCLAT
is 17.11.2026.
11. Issue notice, returnable on 19.11.2026.
12. Dasti service, in addition, is permitted.
13. The NCLAT shall offer its explanation as to why the
6

--- Page 102 ---
matter has not been heard till this date, despite our
specific order referred to above.
14. In the meantime, there shall not be any constitution of
the CoC.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

JAGANNATH MANDANGI ..... APPELLANT(S)
            VERSUS
STATE OF ODISHA & ANR. ETC. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant in these appeals, Jagannath Mandangi, is the
complainant in P.S. Case/First Information Report (FIR) No.
208/2010 dated 23.12.2010 registered with Police Station –
Rayagada, District – Rayagada, Odisha, for offences punishable
under Sections 120B, 302, 201, 364 and 34 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860. The said P.S. Case/FIR was re-registered as FIR No.
10/2011 dated 05.04.2011 by the CID CB, Odisha, Cuttack.  
3. The appellant is aggrieved by the order dated 22.01.2026 passed
by  the  High  Court  of  Orissa  at  Cuttack  in  ABLAPL  Nos.
13154/2024, 12708/2024, 13155/2024, 13820/2024 and 13901/2024,
filed by the private respondents in these appeals, seeking
anticipatory bail in relation to the aforestated P.S. Case/FIR.
By the said order, the High Court expressly opined that it was
1

--- Page 111 ---
not inclined to grant pre-arrest bail to the respondents.
However, having stated so, the High Court directed them to
surrender before the trial Court and move applications for
grant of regular bail within two weeks and upon their doing so,
the trial Court was directed to release each of them on bail,
subject to their furnishing bail bonds of 50,000/- (Rupees₹
fifty thousand only) each with two solvent sureties each of the
like amount.  The High Court also imposed further conditions,
for grant of such relief, to the effect that they should not
indulge in any criminal activity while they were on bail; they
should not harass, threaten or terrorize any of the prosecution
witnesses;  they  should  not  tamper  with  any  prosecution
evidence; they should appear before the trial Court on each and
every  date  fixed  unless  their  personal  appearances  were
dispensed with by the trial Court in accordance with law; and
they should not leave the jurisdiction of the trial Court
without seeking its permission. The High Court also left it
open to the trial Court to impose any other conditions as would
be deemed just and proper.
4. We are informed that acting upon the aforestated directions,
the respondents surrendered and filed applications for grant of
regular  bail  before  the  learned  Sub-Divisional  Judicial
Magistrate (SDJM), Rayagada, and by order dated 30.01.2026, the
learned SDJM, adhered to the directions of the High Court and
granted bail to the respondents.
5. Once the High Court came to the conclusion that no case was
2

--- Page 112 ---
made out for grant of anticipatory bail, it was not for the
High Court to direct as to how the future should unfold. The
High Court not only advised the respondents as to their next
course of action but also decided and dictated the terms on
which they were to be granted bail by the trial Court.  The
positive directions of the High Court, apart from being in
excess of the jurisdiction that it was exercising under Section
438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, completely usurped
the role to be played by the trial Court upon the filing of
regular bail applications at the appropriate stage by the
respondents. In effect, the trial Court was left with no
discretion to adjudicate such bail applications on their own
merits and in accordance with law.
6. The impugned order, to the extent it issued directions in
paragraph 19 thereof is, accordingly, set aside.  The order
shall, however, stand confirmed insofar as rejection of the
respondents’  prayer  for  grant  of  anticipatory  bail  is
concerned. In consequence, the order dated 30.01.2026 passed by
the learned Sub-Divisional Judicial Magistrate, Rayagada, shall
also stand set aside and the respondents shall surrender within
two weeks. The bail bonds and sureties furnished by them shall
stand discharged at that stage. 
7. This order shall, however, not preclude the respondents from
seeking relief at the appropriate stage before the appropriate
forum in accordance with law, consequent upon the rejection of
their anticipatory bail applications by the High Court.
3

--- Page 113 ---
8. The appeals are disposed of in the above terms.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
Criminal Appeal No.2539 of 2026 
 
Gautam Munjal & Anr.                             
    ...Appellant(s) 
 
 
Versus 
 
The State of Himachal Pradesh & Anr.      
  ...Respondent(s) 
 
O R D E R 
 
The appellants are the Director and an employee of a 
Private Limited Company, engaged in the hospitality business. 
The appellants took on lease a property owned by the 2 nd 
respondent’s daughter -in-law, with the building thereon 
suitable for a hotel. The Management and Operations 
Agreement is produced at Annexure P1, by which the lease 
period was stipulated as 20 years. Disputes arose and within a 
period of 2 years, the arrangement fell through and on the 
complaint of the 2nd respondent, an FIR was registered. There 
is an arbitration now initiated by the appellants in terms of the 
agreement. 
2. Learned Senior Counsel for the appellants pointed out 
that the appellants have already vacated the premises and it is 
only due to the constant interference of the 2 nd respondent 

--- Page 118 ---
 
Page 2 of 5 
 
 
herein that the arrangement fell through. It is relevantly 
pointed out that the complaint has been registered by a person 
who is related to the lessor, and not the lessor herself; for that 
reason alone, it should be quashed. Dispute arose in the lease 
transaction and allegation s of theft and mischief are not 
maintainable per se , especially looking at the terms of the 
agreement. 
3. Learned Counsel for the complainant, however, would 
argue that the High Court has correctly not interfered with the 
proceedings.  
4. A reading of the High Court judgment would indicate 
that it had referred elaborately to a number of judgments in 
which this Court refused to quash the criminal proceedings 
but has not referred to the facts in one single case. After 
extracting copiously on the legal principles dilated upon in the 
numerous decisions, abruptly it was stated that the specific 
allegation of damage to the leased property and that of theft of 
articles, does not disclose a civil dispute , and hence , there 
cannot be a quashing of the criminal proceedings. 
5. The First Information Statement (FIS) , as evident from 
Annexure P7, was a complaint to the Chief Minister, which was 
forwarded to the jurisdictional Police Station and registered as 

--- Page 119 ---
 
Page 3 of 5 
 
 
an FIR. The FIS categorically admits that there was an 
agreement but alleges that it was drafted by the 1 st appellant, 
and it heavily favoured the 1 st appellant’s company but only 
executed by the lessors. It is also alleged that the immovable 
fixtures were dismantled and that many of them transported 
out from the site. The property was left in a ruined state, is the 
allegation raised.  
6. The FIS, however, admits that the son of the complainant 
visited the property and was told that modifications were 
being carried out to put in modern amenities in the hotel. 
Though it is contended , that the lessor, complainant’s 
daughter-in-law and her husband, namely complainant’s son, 
visited the local Police Station , the police refused to lodge an 
FIR. However, there is no private complaint lodged by them in 
accordance with the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The 
attempt of the complainant, the 2nd respondent, seems to be to 
influence the investigation, speaking about his age, as also the 
stress and strain the transaction brought on him.  
7. We have looked at the agreement produced as 
Annexure P1, which specifically speaks of a lease of 20 years. 
The lessor had purchased the property with the intention of 
running a hospitality business and not having the requisite 

--- Page 120 ---
 
Page 4 of 5 
 
 
experience, sought the services of the lessee. The lease was of 
the entire property including the building, for the purpose of 
operating and managing a hotel , for which the lessee was 
granted exclusive rights. They were also conferred with the 
unhindered and uninterrupted access 24/7  and the lock -in 
period specified was 20 years. More importantly by Clause 
D11(e), the lessor transferred , to the lessee , the right to 
modify, construct and renovate any part of the building and  
the open outdoor premises as per the business goals of the 
lessee. Pertinent  is also Clause E (11)(h) , that the lessee 
agreed at its own cost to reinstate the said property to its 
original condition, to the extent reasonably possible, at the 
time of vacation of the said property . Hence, the lessee had 
absolute authority to carry out modifications in the building , 
and if at all , the restoration was required it was only after the 
lock-in period of 20 years. Admittedly, the entire arrangement 
met with trouble at its inception itself within two years, leading 
to vacation of the premises by the lessee. The lessee is also 
said to have initiated arbitration proceedings.  
8. The allegations made in the FIS, as we understand, are 
only with respect to the modifications made in the property , 
the right to which the lessor had conceded to the lessee 

--- Page 121 ---
 
Page 5 of 5 
 
 
exclusively and without any hindrance or interference. The 
attempt seems to be to interfere, after the arrangement 
commenced, and that too, at the behest of 2nd respondent who 
had no role in the actual management of the hospitality 
business of the lessor. The complaint at its inception is flawed 
and its continuance would be an abuse and hence, 
unnecessary.   
9. We find absolutely no reason to  permit continuance of 
the criminal proceeding and the proceeding initiated pursuant 
to FIR No.128 of 2024 dated 27.07.2024 registered at the Police 
Station Dhalli, Shimla, is quashed. 
10. The appeal is allowed. 
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

1. Leave granted.
2. These appeals by Union Bank of India and M/s
Arrow Business Development Consultants Pvt. Ltd. (the
Auction Purchaser) are against the Judgment and Order
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in
Writ Petition No. 11132 of 2025 dated 10.12.2025.
3. The  Auction  Purchaser  filed  a  writ  petition
before the High Court for a direction that pursuant to
the  auction  held  on  30.05.2025,  wherein  it  was
declared as the successful bidder, the entire sale
consideration  was  deposited  and  even  the  sale
certificate was issued on 20.06.2025, and therefore a
writ order or direction for grant of possession was
sought.

--- Page 125 ---
2
4. The High Court by the order impugned before us,
dismissed the Writ Petition on the ground that the
auction  followed  by  the  issuance  of  the  Sale
Certificate  are  both  hit  by  the  imposition  and
operation of moratorium in the insolvency proceedings
initiated under Section 96 of the Insolvency and
Bankruptcy Code, 2016 [in short, “the Code”]. The
relevant portion of the judgment of the High Court is
as follows:-
“33. Considering the analysis of the judicial
precedents cited hereinabove to the facts at
hand in the present Writ Petition, the position
that emerges is summarized hereunder:
33(a) The transfer of ownership of the
secured asset in case of a statutory sale
under  SARFAESI  takes  place  upon  the
issuance of the sale certificate. The
amendment to Section 13(8) does not alter
this position. It merely advances the
date of extinguishment of the right of
redemption available to a borrower.
33(b) The loss of the right of redemption
does  not  tantamount  to  the  loss  of
ownership rights. In other words, the
extinguishment of the right of redemption
will not affect ownership rights in the
secured asset.
33(c)  The  sale  conducted  under  the
provisions of the SARFAESI Act in the
present case does not stand completed
since, during the intervening period viz.
from the date of confirmation of sale on
30th May 2025 till the issuance of sale
certificate  on  20th  June  2025,  the
interim-moratorium imposed under Section
96 of the IBC on 9th June 2025, stayed
all proceedings in respect of any debt of
the borrowers.
33(d) In view of the imposition of the
interim-moratorium under Section 96 of

--- Page 126 ---
3
the IBC, payments of the balance six
tranches from sr. nos. (iii) to (viii) as
set out in paragraph 4(h) above could not
have  been  accepted  by  Respondent  No.
1/Bank from the Petitioner.
33(e) Resultantly, the Petitioner is not
the  owner  of  the  secured  asset  and
therefore, not entitled to possession of
the same.”
5. Union Bank of India and Auction Purchaser are in
appeals before this Court. 
6. Heard Mr. P.B. Suresh and Mr. Narender Hooda
learned  senior  counsels,  and  Mr.  Anshuman,  AOR,

7. It is submitted without much contest, that the
auction was conducted and concluded on 30.05.2025, in
which M/s Arrow Business Development Consultants Pvt.
Ltd. became the successful auction purchaser. We are
also informed that the sale was confirmed on the very
same day. However, the petition under Section 94 of
the Code was filed before the Adjudicating Authority
(AA) only on 09.06.2025. This petition under Section
94 is said to have been kept pending without being
numbered for some time and in the meanwhile, the bank
proceeded to issue the sale certificate to the auction
purchaser on 20.06.2025.  
8. It is only after the conclusion of the above-
referred incidents that the Section 94 Petition under
the Code was taken up, and the AA by its order dated
07.08.2025, issued notices on the said application.

--- Page 127 ---
4
There are also subsequent developments. Section 94
petition was taken up for hearing and by its order
dated 02.06.2026, the AA dismissed the proceedings.
9. Having considered the matter in detail, we are of
the  opinion  that  the  proceedings  initiated  under
Section 94 of the Code, which came to be dismissed by
the AA on 02.06.2026, had no effect on the conduct and
conclusion of the auction dated 30.05.2025. We are
also of the opinion that there is no impediment in the
grant of possession to the auction purchaser - M/s
Arrow Business Development Consultants Pvt. Ltd., as
the  sale  certificate  has  already  been  issued  on
20.06.2025.  
10. In view of the above, these appeals are allowed,
and the judgment and order passed by the High Court in
Writ Petition No. 11132 of 2025 dated 10.12.2025 is
set-aside. There shall be a further direction to the
Bank to hand over possession of the auctioned property
to  the  Auction  Purchaser  pursuant  to  the  Sale
Certificate dated 20.06.2025. 
11. We are informed that the respondent(s) have filed
an appeal against the order dated 02.06.2026 before
the NCLAT. If that be so, the appeal will be decided
on its own merits, uninfluenced by the observations
made in these civil appeals. 
12. The civil appeals stand allowed, with the above
directions.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.     OF 2026
(Arising Out of Special Leave Petition (Civil) No.  14322/2025)
UNION OF INDIA & ANR.                             
A-1: Union of India,  Through the Director, Directorate of 
Printing, Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
A-2: The Manager, Government of India Press,
     Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
PRADIP VIJAYKUMAR PAWAR & ORS.  
R-1: Pradip Vijaykumar Pawar
R-2: Shivaji Bandu Rupwate
R-3: Neelima Sakharam Jadhav
R-4: Sachin Rambhau Jadhav
R-5: Nitin Jaywant Pagare
R-6: Sandeep Madhukar Dalvi
                  Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Heard  Ms.  Archana  Pathak  Dave,  learned  ASG  for  the
petitioners,  Mr.  Ashutosh  Thakur,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent(s)  &  Mr.  Shantanu  Sagar,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent No. 3.
2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeal arises out of the order dated 22.07.2024

--- Page 132 ---
2
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in WP No.
9989/2024, by which the order passed by the Central Administrative
Tribunal, Mumbai Bench in OA/564/2015, directing appointment of the
respondents No. 3 and 6 has not been interfered with.
4. Learned ASG submits that both the CAT as well as the High
Court, despite not interfering with the recommendation of the
Central Vigilance Officer for cancellation of recruitment to the
posts of Farash, Chowkidar and Safaiwala, have still directed the
appointment of respondents No. 3 and 6, who had participated in the
said selection process and figured in the list of finally selected
candidates. It is her contention that there is a fundamental error
in the approach both by the CAT and the High Court inasmuch as
when, on the one hand, the process has been held to be vitiated,
making appointments pursuant to that very same exercise cannot be
justified either on facts or in law.
5. She further contends that there were discrepancies after the
interview and practical test and preparation of the final select
list. She states that before actual appointment letters were
issued; the matter was scrutinized by the Central Vigilance Officer
and discrepancies were found indicating illegalities, including
appointment  of  close  relatives  of  persons  who  were  already
employed, recommendation for filling up of posts beyond the numbers
advertised and also on the practical aspect that more than 100
persons were interviewed in a span of two days.
6. Learned ASG points out to the Court that such discrepancies of
facts have never been controverted or found to be incorrect. In

--- Page 133 ---
3
such background, she submits that the exercise as a whole stands
vitiated and the only alternative available is to go through the
exercise afresh, which though on the one hand, technically has been
set aside, on the other hand, by directing the appointment of
respondents No. 3 and 6, the sanctity in principle of the exercise
concerned has also been upheld.
7. Learned counsel for the respondents No. 3 and 6 submits that
there is no fault on the part of the said respondents and once they
had taken part and participated in the interview and practical test
and were allotted marks, there being no error pointed out in such
award of marks, they cannot be placed in the category of others
against whom there may be allegations of nepotism etc. They also
state that for the last almost two decades, the matter has been
pending, and the respondents No. 3 and 6, despite being selected,
have not been given appointment orders and the Court may do justice
to them, and in fact, the same may be tempered with mercy.
8. It is their contention that even with regard to the number of
vacancies advertised and finally recommended, the advertisement
itself indicates that the same is subject to change depending on
future vacancies and it is not the case of the appellants that the
number of candidates recommended exceed the available vacancies.
Winding up their submission, learned counsel submit that in view of
the respondents No. 3 and 6 having suffered for almost two decades
and there being posts available on which they can be accommodated,
and the fact that they have taken part in an exercise for such
recruitment, the Court may, in the facts and circumstances of the

--- Page 134 ---
4
present case, direct the appellants to suitably accommodate them on
any equivalent post.
9. We have considered the entire controversy in depth. The issue
before the Court is simple. It relates to whether once in a process
relating to recruitment to a public post, irregularities of the
nature which have been shown to have taken place in the present
case come to the notice of the Authority and corrective measures
are taken, whether it is proper for the Tribunal or the Court to
interfere on such an issue which in facts are not controverted by
any of the stakeholders or parties concerned.
10.  It is settled law that judicial review is not directed
against the decision, but is confined to the decision making
process. It is equally well settled that administrative decision
cannot and must not be set aside unless it is demonstrated that
there is improper abuse of power.
11. In the present case, as the entire exercise was based purely
on the subjective satisfaction of the interview board along with
the practical test and the discrepancies pointed out in the report
of the Central Vigilance Officer have not been interfered with
either by the CAT or the High Court, still going ahead with the
direction to appoint the respondents No. 3 and 6 appears to be
without any basis. If we uphold such a view taken by the CAT and
the High Court, it would mean that the CAT and the High Court can
substitute their subjective satisfaction for a process in which the
respondents No. 3 and 6 were selected, i.e., only by holding of an
interview and practical test.

--- Page 135 ---
5
12. Moreover, no reasoning has been given either by the CAT or the
High Court as to why the procedure adopted in the case of the
respondents No. 3 and 6 is valid, when clearly the entire process
with regard to all others has been held to be vitiated and the
cancellation of such an exercise upheld.
13. For the reasons aforesaid, the appeal is allowed. The impugned
judgment of the Central Administrative Tribunal dated 12.10.2023
passed in O.A. No.564/2015, as upheld by the High Court vide the
impugned order dated 22.07.2024 in WP No. 9989/2024 is set aside.
The decision of the Authorities to cancel the entire exercise
pursuant to the advertisement  vide Employment News dated 1-7
December, 2007 for the aforesaid three posts is upheld.
14. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.

any useful purpose; hence, we are inclined to accept the
appeal and grant relief as prayed by admitting the appellant
to an order for grant of bail.
8. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned judgment and
order.
9. Appellant  shall  be  released  on  bail,  subject  to
furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of the trial court
and subject to such other terms and conditions as may be
Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.17257/2026 2

--- Page 152 ---
imposed by it.
10. Needless to observe, if released on bail, the appellant
shall  not,  directly  or  indirectly,  by  making  inducement,
threat or promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the
facts of the case from disclosing such facts to the court.
11. In  the  event there  is  any breach of the  terms  and
conditions for grant of bail, the trial court shall be at liberty
to cancel the bail of the appellant.
12. It  is  also  ordered  that  the  appellant  shall  diligently
attend  proceedings  of  the  trial,  unless  exempted.  If  he
abstains from attending the proceedings without justifiable
cause, that could also be seen as breach of the conditions
for  grant  of  bail  and  the  trial  court  will  be  free  to  pass
appropriate orders.
13. Apart from the above, s ince the State has expressed
an apprehension that the appellant is a resident of Madhya
Pradesh  and  may  not  participate  in  the  trial  after  being
released on bail, we direct the appellant to report to the
officer-in-charge/investigating  officer  once  in  every  two
months (starting from 15 th December, 2026 and on the 15 th
of every alternate month), failing which liberty is granted to
Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.17257/2026 3

--- Page 153 ---
bring any such omission to the notice of the trial court and
seek cancellation of bail.
14. We clarify that the observations made in this order and
grant of bail will not be treated as findings on the merits of
the case.
15. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed on the aforesaid
terms.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.         /2026
[@ SLP (Crl.)  No(s).  1012/2024]
BALLARI MAHANAGAR PALIKE              Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
R. DEEPA & ANR.                         Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1.    Leave granted.
2. The present appeal has been filed assailing the
order of the High Court in Criminal Petition No.
101294 of 2019 dated 22.06.2023, wherein the criminal
petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal
Procedure, 1973 (for short, 'CrPC, 1973') was allowed
and  criminal  proceedings  emanating  out  of  Crime
No.61/2019 registered under Section 465, 468, 471,
409 and 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for
short, 'IPC, 1860') was quashed.
3. In the present case, the appellant-complainant
had registered a complaint in Crime No. 61/2019 on
04.07.2019, alleging that the name of accused No.1
was illegally entered in the land register records
with respect to the subject land that belonged to the
appellant-complainant. Thereafter, the said land was
transferred  to  respondent  No.1,  and  later  on  in
favour of respondent No.2.  Before the lodging of the

--- Page 163 ---
2
present complaint, notice was issued to respondent
No.2, containing similar allegations as that of the
complaint averments The High Court in Writ Petition
No. 109347/2019 vide order dated 28.09.2021, quashed
the notice on the premise that the notice issued was
without proper jurisdiction.
4. The  High  Court,  vide  impugned  order  dated
22.06.2023, has allowed the petition under Section
482 CrPC, 1973, quashing the criminal complaint on
the ground that the basis of filing the complaint
i.e. the notice dated 21.01.2019, has already been
quashed by the Coordinate Bench of the High Court.
Aggrieved by the same, the appellant has filed the
present appeal.
5. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
the appellant, the learned Senior counsel appearing
for the private respondent and the learned counsel
appearing for the respondent No.3-State.
6. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  appellant
submits that it is a case of manipulation of land
register records, over the property belonging to the
appellant.  It is further submitted that the High
Court committed an error in quashing the FIR as the
order  passed  in  Writ  Petition  No.109347/2019,
quashing the notice dated 21.01.2019, has got nothing
to do with the criminal proceedings. The incidental
finding that the colluding officers have not been

--- Page 164 ---
3
arrayed as accused in the complaint, also cannot be
sustained in the eyes of law, as the FIR is concerned
with the offence, not with the offenders per se which
will  come  to  light  after  the  completion  of  the
investigation.
7. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the private
respondent submits that it is a civil dispute over
which a criminal colour is being given.  
8. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent
No.3-State submits that in pursuant to the order
passed by this Court on 19.01.2024, the investigation
has been completed and the charge sheet has been
filed  qua the private respondent.  Sanction under
Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
(as it then was), against the officials who allegedly
colluded with the private respondents is awaited.
9. Taking into consideration the above, we are
inclined to set aside the impugned order passed by
the High Court and remit it back as we find that the
reasons assigned cannot be sustained in the eyes of
law.
10. The finding that the order passed by the High
Court in Writ Petition No. 109347/2019, will enure to
the benefit of the private respondent even to the
extent of quashing the criminal proceedings cannot be
sustained in the eyes of law.  Moreover, the other
reasons with respect to the officials having not been

--- Page 165 ---
4
arrayed as accused is awaiting the sanction under
Section  197  CrPC,  1973.  Additionally,  the  charge
sheet has also been filed in the instant case.
11. In such view of the matter, the impugned order
dated 22.06.2023, stands set aside and the matter
stands  remitted  to  the  High  Court  for  fresh
consideration on the merits of the case.
12. Liberty is granted to the private respondent
No.2 to challenge the charge sheet by way of an
application for amendment.
13. Interim  protection  granted  to  the  private
respondent  vide  order  dated  19.01.2024,  shall
continue until the disposal of the main petition by
the High Court.
14. The appeal stands disposed of, accordingly with
the aforesaid liberty.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.
...................J.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
WRIT PETITION [CIVIL] NO.1049/2018
RAHUL SINGH                                Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
HON’BLE HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH & ANR.    Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. The present writ petition has been filed by the
writ  petitioner,  under  Article  32  of  the
Constitution of India, 1950, seeking a direction to
the respondent to appoint the writ petitioner on the
post of Addl. District & Sessions Judge, as per his
selection in the Madhya Pradesh Higher Judiciary
Service (Entry Level) (Direct Recruitment from Bar)
Exam - 2017, along with all consequential benefits
including seniority and other service benefits.
2. It was further prayed to strike down Memo No.
322/Higher  Judiciary  Service  (D.J.)  Examination,
2017,  Jabalpur,  dated  31.01.2018,  and  Memo  No.
385/Registrar  (Examination),  Jabalpur,  dated
21.05.2018,  vide  which,  the  writ  petitioner  was
denied appointment to the said post on the ground
that he does not possess continuous practice of 7
years  on  13.04.2017  i.e.  the  last  date  for
submitting the application.  

--- Page 169 ---
2
3. In the present case, the writ petitioner has a
cumulative experience of about 10 years and 1 month
as an advocate, as well as 1 year and 3 months of
experience  as  a  Judicial  Officer.   The  writ
petitioner has also cleared all the three stages of
the Madhya Pradesh Higher Judicial Services. Despite
this, the respondent(s) have failed to issue an
appointment  letter  for  the  want  of  7  years  of
continuous practice. 
4. We  have  heard  the  learned  Senior  counsel
appearing for the writ petitioner and the learned
counsel appearing for the respondent.
5. The  short  question  that  arises  for  our
consideration  is  as  to  whether  the  continuous
service of seven years will have to be reckoned
along with the tenure of service rendered as a
Judicial Officer.  
6. The said issue is no longer  res integra . A
decision of the Constitution Bench of this Court in
Rejanish K.V. v. K. Deepa -  (2026) 4 SCC 513,
clarifies that the services rendered as a judicial
officer  will  also  have  to  be  included  while
calculating the period of continuous service.  The
relevant paragraph of the said judgment is as under:
“174. In  the  result,  we  answer  the
questions as under:
174.1. Judicial officers who have already

--- Page 170 ---
3
completed seven years in Bar before they
were recruited in the Subordinate Judicial
Service  would  be  entitled  for  being
appointed as a District Judge/Additional
District Judge in the selection process for
the post of District Judges in the direct
recruitment process;
174.2. The eligibility for appointment as a
District Judge/Additional District Judge is
to be seen at the time of application;
174.3. Though  there  is  no  eligibility
prescribed  under  Article  233(2)  for  a
person already in judicial service of the
Union or of the State for being appointed
as District Judge, in order to provide a
level  playing  field,  we  direct  that  a
candidate  applying  as  an  in-service
candidate should have seven years' combined
experience as a judicial officer and an
advocate;
174.4. A person who has been or who is in
judicial  service  and  has  a  combined
experience of seven years or more as an
advocate or a judicial officer would be
eligible for being considered and appointed
as  a  District  Judge/Additional  District
Judge  under  Article  233  of  the

--- Page 171 ---
4
Constitution;
174.5. In order to ensure level playing
field, we further direct that the minimum
age for being considered and appointed as a
District  Judge/Additional  District  Judge
for both advocates and judicial officers
would be 35 years of age as on the date of
application.
174.6. It is held that the view taken in
the  judgments  of  this  Court  right
from Satya  Narain  Singh  [Satya  Narain
Singh v. High Court of Allahabad , (1985) 1
SCC  225]  till  Dheeraj  Mor  [Dheeraj
Mor v. High Court of Delhi , (2020) 7 SCC
401] , which take a view contrary to what
has been held hereinabove do not lay down
the correct proposition of law.”
7. Furthermore, the writ petitioner before us has
been working in the capacity of Additional District
and Sessions Judge since April, 2019, though, by
virtue of an order of this Court dated 22.04.2019.
8. It is not in dispute that the writ petitioner
has been selected on merits. 
9. In such view of the matter, the interim order
passed by this Court, vide order dated 22.04.2019,
is  made  absolute,  and  the  Writ  Petition  stands

--- Page 172 ---
5
allowed, by directing the respondent(s) to continue
the service of the writ petitioner.
10. Needless to state that all benefits shall be

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal No.    /2026
(Arising out of SLP (Crl) No.19298/2026)
Shahjahan & Ors.                                   Appellants
                                VERSUS
Yasmeen & Ors.                                     Respondents
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. The order dated 07.07.2026 passed by the High Court of Uttarakhand at
Nainital is under challenge in this appeal. Facts in brief are as under:-
The respondent no. 1 herein (wife of Mr. Sonu)  filed a petition under
Section 12 of  Protection Of Women From Domestic Violence Act, 2005  before
the jurisdictional Magistrate in Miscellaneous Case No. 85/2022 wherein she
sought  protection  and  award  of  maintenance  of  Rs.25,000/-  per  month  for
herself  and  her  minor  daughter;  restraint  against  alienation  of  the  shared
household and other reliefs as morefully prayed for in the petition which is
annexed as Annexure-P1. On account of the said proceedings not progressing or
in  other  words,  on  account  of  there  being  delay,  she  filed  a  Criminal
Miscellaneous Application No. 684/2025 before the High Court of Uttarakhand
seeking directions for expeditious disposal of Miscellaneous Case No. 85/2022,
contending that proceedings had remained pending for more than two years six
1

--- Page 175 ---
months. 
4. The High Court by Order dated 19.06.2025 admitted the said application
and issued notice to the respondents after observing that their presence was
required. Subsequently, on the next date i.e., on 29.07.2025 the High Court
recorded the absence of Sonu (husband of Yasmeen) and has directed the
applicants to take steps for service of notice through concerned counsulate. The
applicants were also permitted to amend the pleadings regarding the Sonu’s
current  address  and  effect  service  through  electronic  means  including
WhatsApp and e-mail. Subsequently, on 02.07.2026 the High Court observed
that the said Sonu was avoiding the proceedings while residing in Saudi Arabia
and the  learned counsel appearing  for  the  respondents  therein namely the
mother and sisters of Sonu were directed to obtain instructions regarding the
date on which the Sonu would appear, failing which the Court indicated that it
would proceed against respondent Nos. 2 to 4.
5. Subsequently, on 06.07.2026 affidavit came to be filed by Yasmeen and,
as such, non-bailable warrants and proceedings under Section 82 were directed
to be initiated by the competent Court against the concerned respondents in
Criminal Case No. 154/2023. The High Court has also ordered for attachment of
the  property  wherein  the  appellants  herein  namely  the  mother-in-law  and
sisters-in-law  of  the  Yasmeen  were  residing  and  directed  the  jurisdictional
S.H.O. to file a compliance report. Accordingly, the residential property where
appellants are residing is said to have been attached by virtue of which it is
under lock and key and appellants herein have been ousted from the said
property.
6. Learned counsel appearing for the respondents vehemently contends that
the present appeal itself has become infructuous on the ground that High Court
2

--- Page 176 ---
has disposed of Criminal Miscellaneous Application No. 684/2025  vide order
dated 06.10.2026 and as such nothing further remains and it is also observed
by the High Court that the pending proceedings is to be expedited.
7. Had the High Court said or commented upon the impugned order while
passing  the  final  order,  this  Court  would  have  definitely  desisted  from
expressing  any  opinion.  However,  the  impugned  order  though,  which  was
interim in nature is operating and continuing or by virtue of the said order the
jurisdictional police seems to have attached the property, taken possession of
the property  and ousted the appellants from their house, where they were
residing. This is highly impermissible, we say so for the simple reason that
under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, namely,
Section  19(1)(b),  the  jurisdictional  Magistrate  is  empowered  to  remove  the
person from the shared household, the proviso to Section 19(1)(b) is a complete
answer to the present dispute and it reads as under:-
“Provided no order under clause (b) shall be passed against
any person who is a woman.”
8. In the Instant case the appellants herein being the mother-in-law and
sisters-in-law of the complainant-Yasmeen, could not have been ousted from
the  residential  premises  where  they  are  residing  for  non-appearance  of
respondent no.3 (husband of respondent no.1). Even otherwise, the attachment
even if any, would only mean and include the attachment of the property to
prevent any encumbrance being created on the said property or in other words,
the said property becoming custodia legis namely it would come to the custody
of the Court, at the most, this could have been the situation. However, learned
3

--- Page 177 ---
counsel appearing for the appellants has contended and submitted that by
virtue of the attachment the jurisdictional police have locked the premises and
ousted them from the use and occupation of the premises, which is not only
erroneously  but  also  impermissible  as  it  is  contrary  to  the  law  noticed
hereinabove. Hence, we have no hesitation in setting aside the said order and
directing the raising of the attachment forthwith. If, at all the husband of the
complainant namely Mr. Sonu is not attending the Court it is definitely open to
the  wife-Yasmeen  to  take  all  such  steps  to  secure  his  presence  by  filing
appropriate applications before the jurisdictional Magistrate and it is needless to
state that wife who has been now left without any remedy is craving for justice
being meted out to her and as such the jurisdictional Magistrate shall make all
endeavors to expedite the hearing and secure the presence of the husband, if
necessary, through look out notice or such other procedure as established by
law and as permissible.
9. With  these  observations,  we  request  the  trial  Court  to  expedite  the
hearing.
10. In view of the above, the appeal stands disposed of.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
…………………………….J.
(ARAVIND KUMAR)
…….………………………………….J.
(VIPUL M. PANCHOLI)
New Delhi;
October 16, 2026.
