IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.9413/2024
SBUBASHRI SASIKALA DEVI         APPELLANT
                            VERSUS
G.RAJAMANI & ORS.           RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Notice  has  been  served  on  respondent  No.1  –  complainant  as
reflected  from  the  Office  Report,  however,  none  have  entered
appearance on her behalf. The incident being of the year 2019 and six
years  having  elapsed,  we  are  of  the  view  that  keeping  this  appeal
pending would not serve any fruitful purpose and as such by consent of
the learned counsels appearing for the parties, we have taken up this
appeal for final disposal and proceed to dispose of this appeal as under.
2. Heard.
3. This appeal lays a challenge to the order dated 22.01.2024 passed
by the Disciplinary Committee of the Bar Council of India in BCI TR. Case
No.46/2023.
3. The facts in brief which has lead to filing of this appeal are:
3.1 The  appellant  after  completing  her  five  year  Degree  of
Bachelors of Law from Dr. Ambedkar Government Law College,
1

--- Page 181 ---
Puducherry got enrolled as an advocate in the Bar Council of
Tamil Nadu and Puducherry under Roll  No.MS.2029/1992 and
commenced practise.
3.2 Respondent  No.1  –  complainant  lodged  a  criminal
complaint before the Inspector, Crime Branch, Cuddalore against
appellant and one Jayanthi alleging financial improprieties.
3.3 After inquiry, the Crime Branch closed the complaint on
05.12.2019 at the request of the complainant herself finding that
financial  transaction  were  primarily  between  G.Rajamani  and
Jayanthi,  i.e.,  the  complainant  and  Jayanthi.  Thereafter,
respondent No.1 lodged a complaint before the Bar Council of
Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, alleging that appellant had misused
her position as an advocate and induced respondent No.1 to
believe that jobs in Neyveli Lignite Corporation could be secured
by paying bribes to senior officials. Acting on this representation,
the complainant claims to have deposited Rs.11,00,000/- in the
SBI Account of the appellant at Cuddalore Branch, paid further
sum of Rs.7,00,000/- in cash to the intermediaries, Karuppaiah
and Ramesh, and also deposited another sum of Rs.15,00,000/-
in the bank account of the appellant’s friend, Jayanthi, at Trichy.
Complainant further alleged that a total sum of Rs.33,00,000/-
was paid by her but no job as promised was provided nor the
money was refunded though demanded on several occasion. The
2

--- Page 182 ---
complainant annexed the bank challans and receipts and prayed
for appellant being debarred from practicing as an advocate on
the ground of serious professional misconduct.
3.4 The  appellant  herein  filed  reply  statement  and  also
additional  statement. However, the Disciplinary  Committee  of
the Bar Council of Tamil Nadu did not dispose of the matter
within a period of one year as prescribed under the Advocates
Act,  1961,  and  by  deemed  provision,  the  proceedings  stood
transferred to the Bar Council of India.
3.5 Respondent  No.1  –  complainant  filed  proof  of  affidavit
before  the  Disciplinary  Committee  reiterating  the  allegations
made against the appellant on 10.10.2023.
3.6 On 29.01.2024, the appellant filed an application before
the  Bar  Council  of  India  –  respondent  No.2  herein  seeking
recalling  and  reopening  of  the  proceedings  and  sought  for
opportunity  to cross-examine the  complainant and to adduce
evidence  in  her  defence  citing  sufficient  cause  for  non-
appearance. By that time, Disciplinary Committee had already
passed  the  impugned  order  on  22.01.2024  whereunder
punishment of a ban for five (5) years from practicing as an
Advocate  had  been  imposed  on  the  appellant.  Hence,  this
appeal.
3

--- Page 183 ---
4. Though several contentions are raised in this appeal, we do not
propose to go into same as we are taking note of the fact that appellant is
a widow and is ekeing out her livelihood by pursuing her professional
career  and  has  also  been  appointed  as  a  Notary.  Hence,  we  do  not
propose to go into the merits of the case except to the extent of affirming
the findings recorded by the Bar Council of India under the impugned
order  dated  22.01.2024  due  to  contra  material  not  produced  by  the
appellant to rebut the claim made by the complainant. However, taking
note of the fact that appellant is a widow with two young children to care
and the order of suspending the appellant from practicing came into force
from the date of the impugned order, i.e., 22.01.2024 and she having not
practiced for the past two years and eight months as on date would be
sufficient punishment and same would put her on guard. It would also act
as a deterrent so that she would not indulge in such acts in future and
she would continue to discharge her duties of the noble profession of
advocacy. We hope and trust that punishment that has already been
undergone would have brought reformative thinking in her and she would
strive  hard  to  live  up  to  the  expectations  of  the  Bar.  With  this
observation, we modify  the  order  of punishment imposed by the Bar
Council of India under the impugned order from five years to the period of
suspension of practice already undergone till date. With this modification,
the appeal stands allowed in part.
4

--- Page 184 ---
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO(S).                       OF 2026
@SLP (C) NO(S). ___            ____OF 2026
@DIARY NO. 26745 OF 2026
INTERNATIONAL AIR CHARTER OPERATIONS (I)
PVT. LTD. & ORS.                    APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ORS.                                 RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Delay condoned. 
2. Leave granted.
3. These appeals arise out of the judgment and order passed by the High
Court of Delhi in W.P. (C) No. 15231 of 2023 dated 24.11.2023 as well as the
order in Review Petition No. 174 of 2024 dated 30.01.2026.
4. Heard Ms. Akriti Chaubey, learned counsel for the appellants and Mr.
Gurmeet Singh Makker, learned counsel for the respondents.
5. The main issue relates to applicability of Notification dated 03.05.2007
providing exemption from payment of customs duty on import of aircrafts.
However, for some reason or the other, the appellants could not contest their
claim under this notification on merits and their applications or appeals all
through  came  to  be  dismissed  on  technical  reasons.  The  short  facts
necessary for the disposal of the present appeals are as follows.
Page 1 of 6

--- Page 211 ---
6. Pursuant to grant of a No Objection Certificate (NOC) dated 12.12.2007
for import of aircrafts for “Non-Schedule Operations”, the appellants imported
an aircraft after furnishing an undertaking as per Condition No. 104 of the
Notification dated 03.05.2007. Under the said condition, the aircraft was to be
used only for Non-Scheduled Air Transport (passenger) services and in the
event the aircraft was not used for the specified purpose, the appellants were
required to pay an amount equal to the duty payable on such aircraft. The
imported aircraft was cleared on the basis of the exemption from payment of
customs duty under the Notification.
7. Pursuant  to  investigation  initiated  by  the  Commissioner  of  Customs
(Preventive), a Show Cause Notice came to be issued on 17.11.2008, alleging
that the appellants were operating charter services, when their permit was
restricted  to  passenger  services  only.  The  show-cause  culminated  in  the
Order-in-Original  dated  29.06.2009,  holding  the  appellants  liable  to  pay
customs  duty  of  Rs.  6,24,50,565/-,  along  with  an  equivalent  penalty.  The
directors were also held liable to pay Rs. 25 lakh each as penalty.
8. The appellants challenged the order before CESTAT, which disposed of
their  appeals  on  04.01.2017,  on  the  ground  that  there  were  conflicting
decisions of the Tribunal, which were sub-judice before this Court and granted
liberty to the appellants to approach the CESTAT once the question of law is
decided.  Consequently,  the  appellants  filed  appeals  before  this  Court.
However, the pending civil appeals were not decided on merits as the issues
raised therein did not fall within the four corners of Section 130-E of the
Page 2 of 6

--- Page 212 ---
Customs Act. The question of law was left open. In view of the fact that in the
pending  civil  appeals,  this  Court  did  not  decide  the  question  of  law,  the
appellants withdrew their appeals.
9. In the meanwhile, the Assistant Commissioner (Recovery) issued the
first demand notice to the appellants on 30.11.2021. Further, a three-judge
bench of the CESTAT decided the question of law in M/s VRL Logistics Ltd. v.
Commissioner of Customs, Ahmedabad 1, holding that the expression “Non-
Scheduled (Passenger) Services” contained in Condition No. 104 included all
air  transport  services  within  its  scope,  including  charter  services  on
08.08.2022. It is the case of the appellants that the said decision has also
been applied in all similar cases.
10. When  the  Customs  Authority  issued  a  second  demand  notice  on
06.10.2023, the appellants filed a writ petition. The High Court dismissed the
writ petition on 24.11.2023 (impugned order I) holding that, as the appellants
withdrew their Civil Appeals before the Supreme Court unconditionally, the
Order-in-Original  dated  29.06.2009  had  attained  finality,  and  the  demand
notices are only consequential.
11. In the above-referred circumstances, appellants also filed a restoration
application before the CESTAT, pursuant to the liberty given in its order dated
04.01.2017.  The  CESTAT  by  its  order  dated 26.02.2024  held  that  the
appellants  ought  to  have  taken  liberty  from  the  Delhi  High  Court  for
restoration, and in the absence of such liberty, it would be inappropriate for the
1 Customs Appeal No. 74 of 2010-LB
Page 3 of 6

--- Page 213 ---
CESTAT to allow the restoration application and hear the appeal on merits.
The relevant portion is extracted – 
“6. It was for the Writ Petitioners to have taken liberty from the
Delhi High Court to approach the Tribunal for recall of the order
dated 04.01.2017 but such leave was not taken.
7. In  such  circumstances,  it  will  not  be  appropriate  for  the
Tribunal to recall the order and hear the appeal on merits.
8. The applications are, accordingly, rejected. All the pending
Miscellaneous Applications which seek to amend the Restoration
Application stand disposed of.”
12. In the meanwhile, appellants filed a Review Petition against the order of
the learned Single Judge dated 24.11.2023 which came to be dismissed on
30.01.2026 by the second order impugned before us. The relevant portion of
the order is as follows;
“9. Though the learned CESTAT, in its Order dated 04.01.2017,
had left it open to the petitioners to approach the learned CESTAT
again after the final verdict of the Supreme Court, it was stated
that  the  petitioners  must  do  so  “within  the  prescribed  time,  if
advised  so”.  The  appeals  before  the  Supreme  Court  of  the
petitioners  were  withdrawn  by  the  petitioners  on  26.11.2021.
Instead of approaching the learned CESTAT in terms of the liberty
granted vide its Order dated 04.01.2017, the petitioners kept quiet
and filed the present petition on or about 23.11.2023, inter alia
challenging  the  subsequent Demand  Notices  dated  30.11.2021
and 06.10.2023.
10. This Court, therefore, held that once the underlying order,
that is, the Order dated 29.06.2009 passed by the Adjudicating
Authority  was  not  in  challenge,  the  challenge  to  the  Demand
Notices  could  not  be  sustained  and  the  petitioners,  therefore,
could not rely upon the liberty that was granted to the petitioners
vide Order dated 04.01.2017 passed by the learned CESTAT to
maintain the Writ Petition.
11. The  petitioners  thereafter  again  approached  the  learned
CESTAT by filing applications, not seeking to avail the remedy that
has been reserved in the petitioners vide Order dated 04.01.2017,
but to seek a recall of the Order dated 04.01.2017. We fail to
Page 4 of 6

--- Page 214 ---
understand how those applications were even maintainable as the
petitioners  now  are  relying  on  the  very  same  order  dated
04.01.2017 to maintain the present Review Petition.”
13. Having heard Ms. Akriti Chaubey and Mr. Gurmeet Singh Makker, we
are of the opinion that the appellants never had an opportunity of presenting
their case on merits before any forum, at any point of time. Right of appeal
being a precious remedy, Courts shall endeavour to ensure that an aggrieved
party has at least one appellate forum to address its grievances. High Court
dismissed the writ by holding that the appellants did not take the permission of
the Supreme Court for reviving the appeal before CESTAT and the CESTAT
dismissed the application for restoration on the ground that the High Court did
not  give  such  a  liberty.  We  are  of  the  opinion  that  the  mistakes,  if  any,
occurred because of the anxiety of the appellants to somehow or the other
have their appeal restored before CESTAT. These problems can be resolved if
we allow the prayers in the writ petition and revive and restore the appeal
before the CESTAT.
14.  Having considered the matter in detail, we are of the opinion that
interest of justice will be subserved if the appellants’ application for restoration
of the CESTAT Customs Appeal No. 603 of 2009 is allowed and the appellants
are permitted to pursue the statutory appeal. For this purpose, we set aside
the judgment and order of the High Court in Writ Petition No.15231 of 2023
dated 24.11.2023 and RP No.174 of 2024 dated 30.01.2026 and direct that
the Customs Appeal No. 603 of 2009 be restored to its original number.
Page 5 of 6

--- Page 215 ---
15. In view of the above, the Civil Appeals arising out of Special Leave
Petition(s) Diary No. 26745 of 2026 are allowed and consequently Customs
Appeal No. 603 of 2009 on the file of CESTAT is restored to its original
number. We further direct that the CESTAT shall take up and dispose of the
appeal within a period of three months from today.
16. Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Civil) No. 9267 of 2026)
UMESH CHAND JAIN APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
SUKHWATI DEVI & ORS.     RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard Mr. Divyakant Lahoti, learned counsel for the
appellant; Mr. Anand Mishra, learned counsel for
respondents No. 1 to 3/original plaintiffs; and Mr. Aman
Gupta, learned counsel for respondents No. 4 to 10, 12 to
17 and 23 to 27/original defendants.
2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeal arises out of the order passed by
the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Gwalior in Second
Appeal No. 1847 of 2021,  whereby the petition filed by the
appellant under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil
Procedure, 1908, which had been allowed by the Trial Court
and not interfered with by the First Appellate Court, was
reversed and the suit was restored.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the
1

--- Page 247 ---
order impugned clearly shows that it was passed upon
hearing only the appellant therein and most importantly, no
question of law was framed, which has now been held to be
mandatory. It was contended that, besides the parties not
having an opportunity to contest, the allowing of the
Second  Appeal  in  the  aforesaid  background  requires
interference.
5. Learned counsel for contesting respondents No. 1 to
3 submitted that the High Court has basically not passed
any order on merits and to the prejudice of any of the
parties, and further that the same has been done only on
the basis of the stand taken by the appellant himself in
his written statement.
6. Learned counsel for respondents No.  4 to 10, 12 to
17 and 23 to 27 submitted that without even notice, much
less hearing to them, the impugned order has been passed.
He adopted the contention of the learned counsel for the
appellant.
7. Having considered  the matter,  on the  short two
points that no substantial question of law was framed and
the parties were neither noticed nor given an opportunity
of hearing, the impugned order is set aside.
8. The  Second  Appeal  shall  stand  restored  to  its
original number. The High Court shall consider the matter
afresh,  and  if  it  arrives  at  the  conclusion  that  it
2

--- Page 248 ---
requires hearing, then substantial questions of law will be
framed, and the matter shall be disposed of accordingly
after affording an opportunity of hearing to all concerned.
9. We clarify that we have not expressed any opinion on
merits, which are left open for the High Court to decide.
10. It shall be open to the parties concerned to move
before the High Court for expeditious disposal of the
matter. 
11. The appeal is allowed in the above terms.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
Transfer Petition (Crl.)  No.1069/2025
POOJA SRIVASTAVA                                   Petitioner
VERSUS
MANI BHUSHAN VERMA & ORS.                          Respondents
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. This  petition  has  been  filed  for  transfer  of  Criminal  Case  No.
2266/2025 from the Court of Judicial Magistrate, Ranchi, Jharkhand to the
Court of competent jurisdiction at Kanpur, Kanpur Nagar, Uttar Pradesh.
3. This Court having noticed that there is a possibility of settlement the
dispute was referred to the Supreme Court Mediation Centre. Both the
parties appeared and after due deliberations they have entered into a
settlement  agreement.  The  copy  of  which  is  annexed  to  the  report
forwarded by the Mediation Centre.
4. In fact, this matter was listed on 05.10.2026 on which date all the
parties appeared before this Court and submitted that the settlement has
been voluntarily and without any force or threat., The husband who has
been a signatory to the settlement agreement had undertaken under the
agreement file to an application under Article 142 of the Constitution of
India  for  dissolution  of  the  marriage.  The  joint  application  I.A.
No.236770/2026 has been filed accordingly and it is signed by the father-
in-law  of  the  petitioner  as  such  to  enable  the  petitioner  to  file  a
1

--- Page 252 ---
confirmatory affidavit, we had adjourned this matter and accordingly the
affidavit of the husband (Mr. Sumit Kumar) has been filed on 06.10.2026.
A perusal of the said affidavit would indicate that he has confirmed of
having taken part in the mediation proceedings and has reiterated that
the dispute has been settled between him and his wife. The terms of the
settlement as agreed to between the parties read as under:-
“6.    Both the parties hereto have arrived at an amicable settlement
on the following terms and conditions for dissolution of marriage by
mutual consent: - 
A. That  the  parties  have  agreed  that  the  Husband  of  the
petitioner shall pay to the Petitioner-wife a total sum of Rs.
8,51,000/- (Rupees Eight lakh and fifty-one thousand) towards
full  and  final  settlement  of  all  her  claims  towards  her
permanent  alimony,  Stridhan,  maintenance  (past,  present,
future)  and  any  other  claim  whatsoever  before  Hon'ble
Supreme Court of India at the time of hearing of application
under  Article  142  of  The  Constitution  of  India  by  way  of
demand draft drawn in the name of the petitioner- wife. The
payment shall be paid to Ms. Pooja Srivastava in first week of
August, 2026 by way of demand draft. 
B.  It is agreed between the parties that they will move an
application  jointly  before  the Hon'ble  Supreme  Court under
Article 142 of Constitution of India praying for dissolution of
marriage  as  parties  have  been  staying  separately  since
28.07.2024 i.e. for approx. 2 years and there is irretrievable
break down of the marriage.
C.   It is further agreed between the parties that they will also
pray for disposal and quashing of all the aforementioned cases
preferred by the parties against each other and of all the cases
pending between the parties (if any, inadvertently remains not
mentioned in this settlement agreement).
7. That  the  Petitioner  and  her  family  and  Respondent  No.  1
alongwith the Husband of the Petitioner and his family have agreed
that none of them will initiate any other legal action or complaint
against each other or against the family members of each other in
respect  of  their  matrimonial  dispute  in  future.  Petitioner  and  her
family and Respondent No. 1 alongwith the Husband of the Petitioner
and his family undertake to delete all the personal chats from their
phones; photographs exchanged with each other as well as those put
2

--- Page 253 ---
up on any social media platform, and would not post any photographs
of each other or together on any social media platform or against
each other in future or comment on each other's post on the social
media or whatsoever. The Petitioner and her family and Respondent
No. 1 alongwith the Husband of the Petitioner and his family also
agree not to contact each other or their family members in future.
Since the petitioner and the Husband of the Petitioner are in the same
profession, the two undertake that they will not blame each other in
any manner or harm each other professionally.
8. That subject to the aforesaid terms, the parties have resolved
all the disputes amicably in relation to the marriage and have been
left  with  no  claims  against  each  other  or  their  respective  family
members.
9. That by signing this Agreement the parties hereto solemnly
state and affirm that they have no further claims or demands against
each  other  from  hereon  and  in  future,  including  maintenance,
permanent  alimony  and  stridhan  or  any  movable  or  immovable
property and all the disputes and differences have been amicably
settled by the parties hereto through the process of mediation.
10. The parties undertake to abide by the terms and conditions set
out in this Settlement Agreement, which have been arrived with free
will of the parties without any coercion, duress or collusion and parties
undertake not to raise any dispute whatsoever henceforth.”
5. In view of the abovesaid, settlement agreement having been entered into
between the parties voluntarily and the parties being well-educated and being
conversant with the consequences of such settlement, we see no impediment to
accept the same and accordingly, the said settlement stands accepted.
6. In the joint application field i.e., I.A. No.236770/2026 both parties have
sought for grant of divorce by mutual consent under Section 13B of the Hindu
Marriage Act, 1955. As noted hereinabove, the parties being well educated and
in  spite  of  all  efforts  for  re-union  having  failed,   we  are  of  the  view  that
continuation of the marriage would not yield any fruitful result and as such we
deem it proper to accept their prayer and exercise the power vested under
Article 142 of the Constitution of India, the marriage solemnized between the
petitioner and the Sumit Kumar on 12.07.2024 is hereby dissolved by granting
3

--- Page 254 ---
decree of divorce by mutual consent.
7. Registry is directed to draw the decree of divorce accordingly in terms of
the settlement. Both parties have agreed that there are no dues payable from
either  side  and  all  the  proceedings  pending  before  various  courts  stand
disposed of/closed/quashed and continuation thereof would not be warranted.
8. Parties are at liberty to move the jurisdictional court by producing the
copy of this order to enable the jurisdictional courts to close the proceedings for
statistical purposes. Registry to draw the decree of divorce. Both parties to bear
their own costs.
9. Accordingly, the transfer petition stands disposed of.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL Nos.                   OF 2026
[Arising out of  SLP (C) Nos.19090-19091/2026]
  SUMITA GUPTA APPELLANT 
VERSUS
STATE OF U.P. & ORS.      RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. These  appeals  are  directed  against  orders  dated  19 th
December, 2025 and 12 th March, 2026 passed by a Division Bench of
the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench.
3. Incidentally, the appellant was not a party to the proceedings
before the High Court. She was the guarantor for a loan advanced by
the  respondent  no.3-Punjab  National  Bank1 to  Akanksha  Agrawal-
borrower.
4. Upon  the  Bank  taking  steps  under  the  Securitisation  and
Reconstruction  of  Financial  Assets  and  Enforcement  of  Security
Interest Act, 2002 2, the appellant had moved an application under
Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act 3 before the Debts Recovery Tribunal,
Lucknow Bench4.
5. On such application, the DRT passed an interim order on 15 th
July,  2025  restraining  the  Bank  from  taking  steps  for  physical
possession of the secured asset.
6. While such application was pending with a subsisting interim
1  the Bank
2  SARFAESI Act
3  S. A. No.579/2025
4  DRT
1

--- Page 267 ---
order, a writ petition 5 (Anuja Dixit vs. State of U.P. Thru. Chief Secy.
Govt. of U.P. Lko. and 3 Others) came to be disposed of by the order
dated 19th December, 2025. The operative part of such order reads as
follows:
“5. Both  parties  have  submitted  that  there  is  no  proceeding
pending before the Debt Recovery Tribunal and there is no stay
with  regard  to  the  transfer  of  the  property  to  the  auction
purchaser.
6. In  light  of  the  above  submissions,  we  direct  the  police
authorities concerned to provide all assistance required to the
bank authorities to hand over possession of the property to the
auction purchaser/petitioner within a period of four weeks from
date.
7. With the aforesaid observations/directions, the writ petition
stands disposed of.”
7. Despite the fact that the application under Section 17 of the
SARFAESI Act was pending before the DRT, such pendency was not
brought to the notice of the Division Bench by the Bank when the writ
petition of Anuja Dixit came to be disposed of on 19 th December,
2025, as noticed above.
8. However, an application 6 was moved in the disposed of writ
petition. The said application was disposed of by the same Division
Bench of the High Court on 12th March, 2026 by recording as follows:
   “1. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the petitioner. 
2. Paragraph five of the original order of December 19, 2025 is
deleted and substituted with following paragraph : - 
‘Both parties have submitted that there is a proceeding pending
before the Debt Recovery Tribunal but there is no stay before the
Debt Recovery Tribunal with regard to the transfer of property to
the auction purchaser.’
3. It may be further added that the direction given to the Police
authorities in the order dated 19.12.2025 is extended for further
four weeks. 
4.  With  the  above  directions,  the  modification  application  is
allowed. 
5. The order passed in Court today shall be treated as part and
5  Writ-C No.11973 of 2025
6  C.M.A. No. IA 02 of 2026
2

--- Page 268 ---
parcel of the order passed on 19.12.2025.” 
9. Surprisingly, the Bank again did not bring to the notice of the
Division Bench that an order of stay was operative whereby the Bank
was injuncted from taking over possession of the secured assets. Had
such information being disclosed, we wonder whether the Division
Bench would have reiterated the direction for police assistance to be
extended  to  the  Bank  for  taking  over  possession  of  the  secured
assets. 
10. Be that as it may, having regard to the terms of the order of
the  High  Court  dated 19th December, 2025,  the  DRT  vacated the
interim order dated 15th July, 2025 vide order dated 22nd April, 2026.
11. Armed with such orders of the High Court and the DRT, the
Bank dispossessed the appellant and is presently in possession of the
secured asset. Such asset has since been put up for auction.
12. In our considered opinion, the Bank was utterly remiss in not
apprising the Division Bench of pendency of the application filed by
the appellant under Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act as well as the fact
that  there  was  a  subsisting  interim  order  whereby  the  Bank  was
restrained from taking over physical possession of the secured asset.
13. However, now that possession of the secured asset has been
taken over by the Bank, we direct it to restore possession thereof in
favour  of  the  appellant.  She  shall  retain  possession  of  the  same
without creating any encumbrance till such time the application under
Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act is finally disposed of by the DRT.
14. The DRT is encouraged to decide the said application of the
appellant  in  accordance  with  law  as  expeditiously  as  possible,
3

--- Page 269 ---
preferably by the end of February, 2027.
15. Auction notice, if any, issued by the Bank shall remain stayed
until the Section 17 application is disposed of.
16. The impugned orders are modified to the aforesaid extent.
17. The civil appeals are, accordingly, disposed of.
18. All contentions on merits are kept open.
19. We also grant liberty to the appellant to urge before the DRT
her grievance relating to forfeiture of the earnest money deposit by
the  Bank.  Such  grievance  may  be  disposed  of  together  with  the
application under Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act.
20. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

JITENDRA SINGH ..... APPELLANT(S)
            
                      VERSUS
STATE OF CHHATTISGARH ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard Mr. Kaustubh Shukla, learned counsel
for the appellant and Mr. Prashant Singh, learned
counsel for the respondent-State of Chhattisgarh.
3. In this appeal, appellant has taken exception to
the order dated 16.06.2026, passed by the High Court of
Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur (briefly the ‘High Court’
hereinafter) rejecting the bail application of the
appellant.
1

--- Page 272 ---
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  Crime  No.102/2026
registered at Police Station Purani Bhilai in the
District  of  Durg  (Chhattisgarh)  for  the  offence
punishable under Sections 21(b), 27(a) and 8 of the
Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
(briefly the ‘NDPS Act’ hereinafter).
5. Appellant was arrested on 19.02.2026 and has been
in custody since then.
6. As per the prosecution, acting on a confidential
information, police carried out search in the house of
one Prince Kumar and apprehended the 5 accused persons,
including the appellant. From the possession of the
appellant, 350 tablets of Dicyclomine Tramadol weighing
254 grams were recovered.
7. This Court  had  issued  notice  on  31.08.2026,
pursuant to which respondent-State has filed counter
affidavit.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that out
of the 5 accused, 3 co-accused have been granted bail
by the High Court. In so far trial is concerned, only 6
prosecution witnesses have been examined till date out
of the 15 cited witnesses. He, therefore, submits that
appellant should be enlarged on bail.
9. Learned State counsel on the other hand submits
that there is a distinction between the case of the co-
accused and that of the appellant and another who have
2

--- Page 273 ---
been denied bail by the High Court. In so far the
appellant is concerned, 254 grams of the contraband
were recovered from the person of the appellant which
is more than the commercial quantity, which is 250
grams. He also submits that trial is proceeding in the
regular course and having regard to the commercial
quantity seized from the person of the appellant, he
may not be granted bail.
10. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and
on due consideration, we are of the view that a case
for grant of bail is made out. Though the contraband
seized from the appellant is of commercial quantity,
the same is just slightly above the threshold by 4-5
grams. Culpability or otherwise of the appellant shall
be determined in the course of the trial. With 9 more
prosecution witnesses still to be examined, an early
conclusion of the trial does not appear to be a
reasonable possibility.
11. Consequently, we set aside the impugned order of
the High Court dated 16.06.2026 and direct that the
appellant shall be produced before the jurisdictional
special court within a maximum period of 7 days from
today whereafter he shall be released on bail on such
terms and conditions as may be deemed appropriate.
12. Appeal is accordingly allowed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal No.     /2026
(Arising out of SLP (Crl.)  No.10667/2026)
VED PRAKASH TIWARI                      Appellant
                      VERSUS
STATE OF CHHATTISGARH                   Respondent
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant who has been arraigned as an accused in
FIR  No.56/2025  registered  at  Police  Station  Chhawni,
District  Durg  (C.G.)  for  the  offence  punishable  under
Section  21(C)  of  the  Narcotic  Drugs  and  Pyschotropic
Substances  Act,  1985  (for  short  “NDPS”)  is  seeking  for
being enlarged on bail.
4. On  01.02.2025  the  jurisdictional  police  received  a
secret information that appellant along with other persons
selling narcotics tablets near Baikunthdha, Podium using a
Pulsar motorcycle. The police accordingly, conducted a raid
SLP (Crl.)  No.10667/2026             Page   1   out of3

--- Page 302 ---
and  recovered  four  boxes  containing  8  strips  each  of
Alprazolam tablet, total 1200 tablets from the possession of
the appellant. The prosecution alleges that the contraband
was recovered from his possession constituted commercial
quantity under the NDPS Act.
5.  We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties. The learned counsel appearing for the appellant
contends  that  vehicle  was  seized  by  the  police  in
connection with Crime No. 56/2025 registered at Chhawni
Police Station, the appellant being the registered owner of
the seized motorcyle.  It is contended that the mandatory
procedural safeguards contemplated under Section 42 and
50 of NDPS Act was not complied with during search and
seizure. It is also contended that no independent witnesses
were associated during the recovery from a public place
rendering the prosecution case doubtful. Hence, appellant
seeks for being enlarged on bail.
6. Per  contra,  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent-State submit that contraband was seized from
the conscious possession of the appellant and, as such, he
is not entitled for the discretionary relief at the hands of
SLP (Crl.)  No.10667/2026             Page   2   out of3

--- Page 303 ---
this Court.
7. Having heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties  and  on  perusal  of  the  records,  we  notice  that
appellant has no criminal antecedents and chargesheet has
been filed and trial is in progress. Hence, we are of the
considered view that appellant is entitled to be released on
bail.  The  fact  that  the  appellant  is  in  custody  from
01.02.2025 would also persuade us to grant the prayer
sought for. Hence, appeal is allowed, impugned order is set
aside and appellant is ordered to be released on bail on
such terms and conditions as the jurisdictional Court deems
fit to impose.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant(s) before this Court has filed the
present appeal(s), being aggrieved by the order dated
12.09.2023 in CRL MP(MD) No. 12237 of 2023 in CRL A(MD) No.
347 of 2023 and impugned final common judgment dated
03.10.2023 passed by the Madurai Bench of Madras High Court
in CRL A(MD) No. 347 of 2023 and CRL A(MD) No. 577 of 2023,
whereby the conviction and sentence of 10 years’ rigorous
imprisonment along with fine of Rs. 1,00,000/- imposed upon
the appellant (s), under Sections 8(c) read with Section
20(b)(ii)(C)  of  the  Narcotic  Drugs  and  Psychotropic
Substances Act, 1985 , by the II-Additional Special Court
for EC and NDPS Act cases, Madurai in C.C. No. 267 of 2020,
were affirmed.
2

--- Page 316 ---
3. Learned  Senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant(s) submits that there is every likelihood of the
appellant(s)  being  acquitted  in  the  appeal(s).  It  is
submitted that allegedly 25 kg of ganja packed in two sacks
(containing 15 kg and 10 kg respectively) was recovered
from the appellant(s) as well as the co-accused. Learned
Senior  counsel  further  points  out  that  out  of  the
substantive sentence of 10 years, the appellant(s) has
already  undergone  about  six  years  of  actual  rigorous
imprisonment, and the final hearing of the appeal is likely
to take considerable time.
4. On the other hand, learned counsel appearing for the
respondent-State has vehemently opposed the prayer for
suspension  of  sentence,  submitting  that  a
commercial/contraband  quantity  of  25  kg  of  ganja was
recovered from the appellant(s) and co-accused. It is
further contended that on the basis of the statements of
the prosecution witnesses, no case for acquittal is made
out.
5. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and
upon perusal of the materials on record, and taking into
consideration the period of incarceration already undergone
by the appellant(s) as well as the fact that the appeal is
not likely to be heard in the near future, this Court is of
3

--- Page 317 ---
the opinion that the prayer for suspension of sentence
deserves to be allowed. Accordingly, the prayer is allowed.
6. The  appellant(s)  is  accordingly  directed  to  be
released on bail during the pendency of the appeal, subject
to such terms and conditions as may be imposed by the Trial
Court.
7. List the appeals in due course.

4. By our order referred to above, we had made an earnest
request to the NCLAT to ensure that the main matter is heard
on 23.07.2026. We made this request to the NCLAT considering
that the NCLT had reserved its order insofar as Section 7
IBC application is concerned.
5. Today, the learned senior counsel appearing for the
applicant brought to our notice that the NCLAT has not heard
the matter till this date. They also brought to our notice
that in the meantime, the order that was reserved by the
NCLT has been pronounced and Section 7 IBC application has
been admitted.
6. We are quite disturbed with the manner in which the
NCLAT has conducted itself in the present litigation. The
request made is out of deference to their position and to
ensure that the judicial office they hold is not belittled
in any manner.
7. When the Supreme Court makes a request to any Court or
Tribunal, it has to be construed as a direction and not just
a request. It is one thing that the Supreme Court earnestly
requests in the hope that the Court or the Tribunal would
abide by the request and do the needful. However, today, we
3

--- Page 329 ---
make it very clear that if there is any request made by the
Supreme Court to any Court or Tribunal, the same shall be
treated as a direction and non-compliance of such direction
shall be looked into very seriously.
8. We are informed that the next date fixed by the NCLAT
is 17.11.2026.
9. Issue notice, returnable on 19.11.2026.
10. Dasti service, in addition, is permitted.
11. The NCLAT shall offer its explanation as to why the
matter has not been heard till this date, despite our
specific order referred to above.
12. In the meantime, there shall not be any constitution of
the CoC.

VERSUS
STATE OF CHHATTISGARH      ...RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. The present appeal calls in question two issues.  The
first  issue  is  with  respect  to  the  condition(s)
imposed by the High Court for release of the vehicle
i.e., Mahindra Thar and the other is with respect to
release of two mobile phones.
3. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties. 
4. On the first issue, we are inclined to modify the
condition imposed vide impugned order passed by the
High Court to the extent that the bond for the sum of
Rs.15,00,000/- and the Bank Guarantee for the sum of
Rs.10,00,000/-  both  shall  stand  reduced  to
Rs.1,00,000/- each. 
5. That leaves us to the second issue. 

--- Page 368 ---
6. It has been submitted that the passwords of the two
mobile phones have been furnished by the appellant(s)
and the mobile phones have been sent to Forensic
Science Laboratory (FSL) for examination. 
7. We direct that after required examination by FSL, the
mobile phones shall be returned to the appellants,
subject to the condition that the mobile phones shall
be produced before the trial Court, as and when
required.
8. Accordingly, the impugned order stands modified and
the appeal stands allowed in the aforesaid terms.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

KNR-SLMI (JOINT VENTURE) APPELLANT(S)
       VERSUS
ORIENTAL INSURANCE COMPANY LTD. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties, we are of
the opinion that the National Consumer Disputes Resolution
Commission1, New Delhi, was not justified in restricting the
appellant’s entitlement to interest only from the date of
repudiation, that is, 12.06.2019, inasmuch as the cause of
action arose in the year 2013 itself and despite the appellant
submitting its claim during that year, the repudiation of that
claim took place nearly six years later. 
2. We  find  that  the  surveyor  appointed  by  the  respondent-
Insurance Company submitted a report as long back as on
06.03.2014 and there was no reason why the Insurance Company
should have slept over the matter for another five years. 
3. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed in part, directing payment
of interest at the rate of 7% per annum from 06.03.2014 upon
1   For short ‘NCDRC’
1

--- Page 383 ---
the assessed loss amount of 2,49,69,435/- (Rupees two crores₹
forty nine lakhs sixty nine thousand four hundred thirty five
only) till the date of actual payment of the said amount. 
4. The interest already paid pursuant to the judgment/order of
the  NCDRC,  that  is,  from  12.06.2019,  may  be  deducted
therefrom.  
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. A detailed affidavit has been filed on behalf of the
appellant offering alternative land to the respondents.
2. However, it is seen that the land offered is not
government land as on date, nor does it belong to the
Transmission Corporation of Andhra Pradesh Limited, but is
owned by private individuals. It is unfortunate that the
State  Government  /  Transmission  Corporation  of  Andhra
Pradesh Limited, which owns large parcels of land, has not
offered any government land to the respondents, and the
appellant seeks one year's time to acquire and hand over
the private land reflected in the affidavit.
3. The  offer  so  made  is  not  acceptable  to  the
respondents. Learned Senior counsel for the respondents
submits  that  if  the  provisions  of  the  Right  to  Fair
Compensation  and  Transparency  in  Land  Acquisition,
Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 are applied, the
liability of the State would exceed Rs. 154 crores. The
respondents have categorically stated that they are not
agreeable  to  accepting  alternative  land  and  seek
compensation in accordance with law.
4. The appellant is directed to place on record an
offer indicating the monetary compensation it proposes to
pay to the respondents in lieu of the land acquired. Let
the  said  offer  be  placed  on  record  within  one  week
2

ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the petitioner(s)
and learned counsel for Respondent No.2-wife.
2. This  Transfer  Petition  has  been  filed  by  the
petitioner(s) seeking transfer of Case No.112171 of 2025
titled as “State versus Udit Dikshit”, pending before the
Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate, Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh
to the District & Sessions Court, Karkardooma Courts, East
Delhi.
3. It appears that Respondent No.2-wife had lodged the
aforesaid complaint, alleging torture and ill treatment
following  her  marriage  with  petitioner  No.1-husband.
Accordingly, the aforesaid case has been registered under
Sections 498A/323/506 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for
short,  ‘IPC’)  read  with  Sections  3/4  of  the  Dowry
Prohibition Act, 1961.
4. On a query by the Court, learned counsel for the
petitioner(s) submits that petitioner No.1-husband is a
resident of Delhi and the instant case has been filed only
1

--- Page 407 ---
to  cause  harassment  to  him.  He  also  submits  that
Respondent No.2-wife is now a resident of Delhi but her
parental home is at Lucknow.
5. Petitioner(s) are accused in the aforesaid case. For
convenience of an accused, a criminal case cannot be
transferred from one place to other.
6. We see no good reason to entertain the Transfer
Petition.
7. Accordingly, the Transfer Petition is dismissed.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

For Respondent(s) :Ms. Sugandha Jain, SC, Adv.
                   Mr. Prabodh Kumar- 2406, AOR
                   
                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. These three petitions seek leave to impugn a common judgment
and order of the High Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur dated
25.03.2026 which has been passed in three connected criminal
appeals i.e. Criminal Appeal Nos. 869/2011, 954/2011 and 51/2026.
The aforesaid criminal appeals are by the brother-in-law, father-
in-law, mother-in-law and husband of the deceased who were all
accused of offences punishable under Sections 498A and 304B of the
Indian  Penal  Code,  1860  (for  short  ‘IPC’).  Besides,  in  the
alternative,  they  were  charged  for  offences  punishable  under
Sections 302 and 306 of IPC.
2. The bother-in-law was convicted only under Section 498A IPC
whereas  the  mother-in-law,  father-in-law  and  husband  of  the
deceased were convicted under Sections 498A and 304B IPC.
3. Against his conviction, the bother-in-law of the deceased
filed a separate petition before this Court, which was dismissed by
2

--- Page 462 ---
a  co-ordinate  Bench  presided  by  Hon’ble  Mrs.  Justice  B.V.
Nagarathna, vide order dated 29.05.2026.
4. Prima facie, it appears, the evidence qua demand of dowry and
harassment in connection therewith is common against all the
accused. In such circumstances, having regard to the fact that one
of the co-convict’s SLP has been dismissed by a co-ordinate Bench,
and the Presiding Judge of that Bench is still a sitting Judge of
this Court, we are of the view that it would be appropriate that
these matters are placed before Hon’ble the Chief Justice of India

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1.  The petitioner before this Court has filed this
present special leave petition for grant of bail/suspension
of  sentence.  He  has  been  convicted  for  the  offences
punishable under Sections 8, 15(c) & 25 of the NDPS Act and
PETITION(S) FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (CRL.)  NO(S).  13196/2026

--- Page 730 ---
2
has been awarded 10 years of rigorous imprisonment. The
petitioner’s appeal is pending before the High Court of
Jharkhand  at  Ranchi,  however,  his  application  for
suspension of sentence has been rejected by impunged order
dated 29.06.2026.
2.  Learned counsel for the petitioner has argued before
this Court that a co-accused has also been awarded a
sentence of 10 years of rigorous imprisonment and has been
granted bail and the petitioner is also identically placed.
Learned counsel for the respondent-State has not disputed
the aforesaid fact.
3. This Court keeping in the view the fact that the co-
accused has already been granted bail by the High Court and
the final hearing of the appeal will take a long time is of
the opinion that the prayer for bail/suspension of sentence
deserves to be allowed and it is accordingly allowed.
4. The petitioner is accordingly directed to be released
on bail during the pendency of the special leave petition,
subject to such terms and conditions as may be imposed by
the Trial Court.
5. List the matter in due course.

2. The present appeal is already admitted and tagged to the

described as simple in nature. Obviously,
the assailant is accused No.1 and none of
present  petitioners.  When  no  specific
allegations are made against any of these
petitioners  and  moreover  when  there  is
inordinate delay in lodging the complaint
as it was lodged on 16.08.2023, while the
incident  said  to  have  occurred  on
28.05.2023,  I  am  of  the  opinion  that,
deliberately these petitioners being the
relatives  of  accused  No.1,  are
unnecessarily roped in, which is in abuse
of process of law. Hence, I am of the
opinion  that  the  criminal  proceedings
initiated against the petitioners/accused
Nos.2 to 7 is liable to be quashed.
5. We do not find any good reason to interfere with the
finding of the High Court.
6. Accordingly, the Special Leave Petition is dismissed.
 (IRAMNAZ)                                       (CHETNA BALOONI)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             COURT MASTER (NSH)

2
       UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Though various grounds were raised in the Special Leave
Petition, we were inclined to examine only one issue, that is to
see if the integrity of the proceeding before the High Court has in
any way been compromised. This is for the reason that one of the
Judges of the Division Bench which passed the impugned order
appeared as a counsel at one stage of the proceedings. 
2. Having examined the matter in detail, it is seen that the
learned Judge’s appearance was noticed as Deputy Solicitor General
representing Union of India. Union of India was only a non-
contesting formal party to the proceedings.
3. Having considered the matter in detail, we are satisfied that
the appearance of the learned Judge as Deputy Solicitor General of
India, as he then was, was given in a routine manner. We are of the
opinion that the said appearance of the learned Judge has no
bearing on the integrity of the proceedings. The Special Leave
Petition is dismissed. 
4. In the facts and circumstances of the case, at the request of
the parties, the payment of fees as for nominating the arbitrator
is extended by 5 weeks from today.
5. Pending interlocutory application(s), if any, is/are disposed
of.

1. The petitioner-wife has filed the petition under
Section 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 before this
Court seeking transfer of M.C. No. 598/2020 titled as
“Sasaank Botlaguduru vs. Botlaguduru Sree Suneetha @ Alanka
Sree Suneetha” pending before the Principal Judge, Family
Court, Bangalore, Karnataka to the Court of Principal
Judge, Family Court, Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh.
2. Having  heard  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
parties and taking into consideration the grounds taken in
the transfer petition, we are not inclined to transfer the
case sought for. The Transfer Petition is, accordingly,
dismissed.
3. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
Petition for Special Leave to Appeal(Crl.) No.19293/2026
[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated 25-09-2026
in CRLMBA No. 26426/2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad]
SHARAD GUPTA                                     Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF U.P. & ANR.                             Respondent(s)
(IA No. 310213/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING C/C OF THE IMPUGNED
JUDGMENT & IA No. 310215/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.)
 
Date : 26-10-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE J.B. PARDIWALA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE K. VINOD CHANDRAN
For Petitioner(s) : 
                   Mr. Ajit Sinha, Sr. Adv.
                   Mr. Sanjeev Agarwal- 1795, AOR
                   Mr. Ekansh Agarwal, Adv.                   
For Respondent(s) : 
Upon hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
O R D E R
1. Exemption Applications are allowed.
2. The Petitioner is aggrieved with the rejection of regular bail
by the High Court. The regular bail application filed without
surrender  was  held  to  be  not  maintainable  in  law  and  the
application was rightly rejected, even according to us.
3. Sri Ajit Sinha, Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner,
however, points out that despite an order directing the application
to move for bail within a period of 45 days, the application moved
was dismissed as per Annexure P16. 
4. We are not convinced that the accused followed the procedure,
as would be clear from Annexure P15 Order of the High Court.
Therein, an anticipatory bail application was withdrawn and a

--- Page 1032 ---
2
submission was made that a bail application will be moved before
the Trial Court and sought protection in the meanwhile. The High
Court granted the prayer and directed the petitioner to apply for
bail through Counsel within a period of 45 days from the date of
that order, during which period, coercive steps were also stayed. 
5. However, the petitioner again filed an anticipatory bail
application without appearing before the Court and moving a bail
application. The FIR is of the year 2016; the petitioner has been
evading appearance for all this while. 
6. In such circumstances, we are not inclined to exercise our
discretion in favour of the petitioner, nor can we grant regular
bail, as rightly pointed out by the High Court, without actual
surrender. However, considering the nature of the offence, the
petitioner is directed to appear before the Trial Court within a
period of four weeks from today; which was the actual intention
behind Annexure 15 order.
7. Considering the fact that the complaint is filed by the Drug
Inspector, the petitioner shall move an application for bail, in
advance, to ensure notice and due instructions from the Drug
Inspector/Complainant. On the next posting date, the petitioner
shall appear before the Special Judge, (Drugs & Cosmetics Act)/
Additional Session Judge, Court No. 9, District Agra, U.P. upon
which, we direct the said Court to consider the bail application on
the same day after hearing the Complainant too, on the same day. We
make it clear that there need not be a consideration as directed,
if the petitioner or any of them do not appear before the Special
Court.
8. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of with the above
direction.
9. Pending applications, if any, shall stand rejected.
 (VISHAL ANAND)                                    (POOJA SHARMA)
DEPUTY REGISTRAR                                 COURT MASTER (NSH)

Mr. Aviraj Pandey, Adv.
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay in filing this special leave petition is
condoned.
2. The contention of the learned counsel for the
petitioner is that the High Court in paragraphs 28
and 29 of the impugned order has wrongly observed
that  the  petitioner  is  charged  for  an  offence
1

--- Page 1082 ---
punishable under Section 409 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860 and that the offence punishable under
Section 409 IPC is made out. It has been submitted
that the petitioner had applied for discharge before
the trial court. The trial court vide its order dated
12.12.2025 had specifically found offence punishable
under Sections 406 and 409 of IPC not made out and
the petitioner was discharged from the said charge.
In such circumstances, since the revision petition
was by the petitioner, not by the State, and the
prayer in the revision was limited to questioning the
applicability of the charging Sections i.e. Sections
420/34 of IPC and Section 3 of the Maharashtra
Protection of Interest of Depositors (In Financial
Establishments) Act, 1999 (for short ‘MPID Act’), the
High Court could not have observed that the offence
punishable under Section 409 of IPC is made out.
3. Issue notice, limited to the aforesaid aspect,
returnable in four weeks.  
(CHETAN ARORA)                                  (SAPNA BANSAL)

For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
IA No. 315345/2026
1. Looking to the fact that Section 307 IPC was watered down to a
conviction under Section 326 IPC where fracture took place on a
non-vital part of the body, the application for exemption from
surrendering stands allowed till the first date of listing of the
proceedings before the Court.
2. The  petitioner,  for  the  time  being,  is  exempted  from
surrendering subject to his furnishing bail bonds of Rs.50,000/- to

Date : 26-10-2026 These petitions were called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE DIPANKAR DATTA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SHEEL NAGU
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Siddharth Dave, Sr. Adv.
                   Dr. Alex Joseph- 1928, AOR
                   Ms. Dhruvi Sikarwar, Adv.
                   Mr. Nayan Dham, Adv.
                   Mrs. Sangeetha Mr, Adv.
                                      
For Respondent(s) :Ms. Rooh-e-Hina Dua- 3014, AOR
                   Ms. Shrutika Garg, Adv.
                   Ms. Dhwani Arora, Adv.                          
          Upon hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Since the High Court was approached at a point of time when
83 out of the proposed more than 300 witnesses had been examined
by the prosecution, we are of the considered opinion that this is not a
fit and proper case to exercise jurisdiction under Article 136 of the
Constitution of India, hence, the special leave petitions are dismissed.
